Autodesk's Flow Studio has moved beyond simply generating video from prompts. The new workflow targets something generative AI has rarely offered: control a director can actually touch.

blocks.cap: Autodesk Flow Studio's new 3D Editor and Canvas.

blocks.x: This episode of fxpodcast featured Nikola Todorovic, Wonder Dynamics co-founder now at Autodesk. The topic was Flow Studio's new 3D Editor and Canvas, which bundle together hands-on 3D scene building and the output of generative 2D video models.

The design intent isn't making a film from a single prompt. It's inserting AI into the production pipeline. It targets both individual filmmakers working in crews of three to five and much larger studios.

The premise is simple. Filmmakers direct in three dimensions: they place the camera, block actors, refine performances, and decide where a shot lands. Trying to convey all of that through text prompts or marks on a flat 2D image was always going to run into obvious limits.

In the 3D Editor, a shot is assembled from characters, animation, motion capture data, camera tracks, and generated environments. A performance can come from one reference clip, camera movement from another, or the camera can be keyframed directly. Spatially consistent environments, such as Gaussian splat worlds made with World Labs' Marble, are used for blocking, layout, and camera design.

Next comes Canvas, a node-based 2D environment where the final image is generated and refined. This is where today's AI video models already do well: integrating lighting, atmosphere, simulation effects, and a cinematic finish.

The 3D scene itself doesn't produce the final pixels. It sets the performance, staging, composition, and camera movement that guide the generated result. If speed matters, you can stay inside Canvas alone, and move into 3D only when a shot needs precise direction.

Todorovic talks about generative AI's 80/20 rule. A prompt and an AI model get the first 80 percent of an image done astonishingly fast. The problem comes when a director asks for a precise fix: move this object, change that performance, adjust the camera path, but don't touch what already looks good.

That last 20 percent is where prompt-only work becomes unpredictable. It's also where the “AI slop” criticism comes from. Without a way to reach directly into the shot, what artists get back is whatever interpretation the model judged statistically safest.

Hollywood filmmakers, executives, and actors have been meeting privately with Silicon Valley executives for the past three years, trying to settle a question the industry has carried for a long time: where does AI become useful within a creative process that people control?

The meetings were first convened by Lucasfilm's Kathleen Kennedy and American Film Institute dean Susan Ruskin, in November 2023. At a gathering of around 120 people last weekend, the coalition arrived at a single framework. It maps out where AI has already entered the film industry, sets out how people can retain control in the remaining use cases, and addresses the scope for AI to produce copyrightable work.

The framework was first reported by The Ankler. According to Page Six Hollywood, attendees included actor and InterPositive co-founder Ben Affleck, A24 partner Scott Belsky, CAA agent Greg Siegel, Paramount+ originals executive Chris Parnell, “Stutz” producer Diane Becker, 30 Ninjas CEO Zade Weintraub, and director John Avnet.

The document is called Human Generative Workflows. In its first public statement, the coalition said it was meant to “spark industry discussion and provide a shared vocabulary for thinking about authorship in the generative AI era.” It drew a line against tackling more urgent issues like how models are trained or how jobs will be affected.

“This conversation is bigger than AI,” the coalition said of the framework. “The future of entertainment won't be built by AI alone. It will be built by the choices we make about how to integrate AI into the creative process.”

The document first takes issue with how the industry talks about AI today, pointing out that the abbreviation “AI” covers everything from DaVinci Resolve's color grading assist to prompt-based synthetic performances that replace actors, in a single breath. So it proposes a classification system that sorts the AI already on set into categories, one that could eventually be used with audiences as well.
It also lists machine-learning-based tools that already produce copyrightable work. Items on the list of AI-assisted tasks include “upscaling and sharpening” and “markerless motion capture.”

The dividing line is AI-generated assets like voices and likenesses. The document defines these as tools that “replace human creative work,” distinguishing between “a set of tools and processes that serve a human's creative vision, versus prompt-based generative tools that replace it.” In the coalition's judgment, this latter category does not carry copyright.

Lineo, aimed at commercial production, has released a production management platform that runs a job from first bid to final wrap in one place. It covers budgets, calendars, bid letters, bid packages, purchase orders, payroll, and petty cash ledgers, with actual spend visible to the whole team in real time. It was built by working producers Corwin Carroll, Erik McCaslin, and Austin Beckford.

“Commercial production has never been squeezed harder than it is now. Deliverables keep growing, budgets keep shrinking,” says co-founder Carroll. “The only way out is working smarter. After more than a year of use by executive producers, line producers, and coordinators, Lineo has cut bidding time, which lets us work three times faster. We put that saved time back into the work itself.”

Production teams usually run on a dozen or so tools that don't talk to each other. Lineo says it has folded all of that into a single operating screen. At the bidding stage, producers build real-time, collaboratively edited budgets using the AICP/APA formats they already use, with support for the world's top 20 currencies. The planning stage brings calendars and resources onto one screen so the whole team sees the same picture.

At the package stage, you pull in a past budget, polish the bid letter with AI, brand the calendar, and export a single PDF bid package without ever leaving the app. At the settlement stage, AI scans and parses purchase orders, payroll, and petty cash to log them, and the result flows into actual spend figures that accounting software can read.

Production Assistant is an AI that pulls this job's data on the spot. “List unpaid purchase orders over $5,000.” “What's the deadline for the Taft-Hartley filing?” You can upload bid specs, scripts, and treatments and ask directly. Outside the assistant too, AI reads invoices, payroll documents, and receipts to fill in purchase order, payroll, and petty cash ledgers on its own, removing the window that used to produce the most mistakes at wrap.

The macOS desktop app runs fully offline. You can use it on a plane or on location and it syncs the moment you're back online. Security includes end-to-end encryption, tenant isolation with row-level permissions, payments handled only through Stripe, AI document processing that retains no data, and personal information that's automatically erased.

Pricing is split between an individual-producer plan and a production-team plan. Coming add-ons include ReelFlow, for sharing reels and libraries with collaborators, and Accounting Sync, for exporting directly to Xero and QuickBooks.

“After running a production company for a long time, what I needed most was for owners, executives, and accounting to see the situation in real time,” explains co-founder Beckford. “Because finding out a month later, there's nothing left you can do about it.”

Moonbug Entertainment, the children's content studio behind Cocomelon, Little Baby Bum, Blippi and Mia's Magic Playground, has asked its in-house animators to try using AI when making its shows, according to 404 Media.

A generative AI policy and a 'Studio AI Bible' obtained by 404 Media show the company is still in the early stages of experimentation, with multiple layers of guardrails set up because of the legal and copyright issues that come with deeper AI use.

“Keep a human in the loop when using AI. AI is a tool to assist the artist, not the artist,” one part of the guidelines reads. “Copyright only applies to human-made work. So the final output must contain substantial human creativity. Core IP — meaning primary characters, signature worlds, and important backgrounds — must reflect human creative intent.”

Moonbug's shows have hundreds of millions of subscribers on YouTube. A Cocomelon spinoff airs on Netflix, a Cocomelon movie with Universal is in the works, and the series is moving to Disney+ next year.

A spokesperson told 404 Media that “generative AI is not currently used in our content episodes.” The guidelines ban AI from generating major creative elements from scratch, such as new characters, core storylines, or song lyrics. All output goes through human-led quality control, including frame-by-frame visual review, the spokesperson said.

The guidelines allow AI in brainstorming, scriptwriting, storyboarding, design and animation, but attach conditions at every stage. Altering a voice actor's or performer's delivery without legal sign-off is not allowed. AI can polish a human-written draft but cannot ghostwrite one. Parts considered the 'soul' of the story — character arcs, key twists, and song lyrics — are left to humans. Feeding a 100% AI-made design straight into the production pipeline is also blocked.

The details are quite strict. AI can be used for 'generic' background designs and textures — like trees or furniture — swapping character outfits, and turning a human-drawn 2D character into a 3D turnaround. New characters are, in principle, made by humans. The same goes for unique props that get major attention in a series, like a clubhouse.

Each tool must receive individual legal approval. Employees first test tools on non-Moonbug-IP test assets. All AI use, including prompts, is logged and kept, and AI-made assets are stored in separate folders from human-made ones. The company calls this approach 'provenance and isolation.'

The prompt guide says to upload a human-drawn sketch or Moonbug-owned IP as a structural reference, then use AI to add texture and lighting. Text-to-image prompts are banned outside brainstorming and research. Style mimicry, such as “in the style of Pixar” or “in the style of Ghibli,” is also blocked. Instead, the guidance calls for descriptive language, like “hand-painted watercolor feel.”
Last May, IATSE workers on the live-action Cocomelon spinoff went on strike over wages and benefits.
“We see AI as a tool that expands what talented creators can do, not something that replaces the people who make the stories,” the spokesperson said.

Avid Media Composer 2026.8 already caused a stir with the announcement that third-party bin locking is effectively being moved to a premium tier starting with this version. Now that the full feature set has been revealed, there turns out to be more in this release than that.

The release date is September 1. Avid says 2026.8 expands collaboration and storage options for Shared Projects. Avid NEXIS can now be used with Shared Projects starting at the Standard tier. As previously reported, the Enterprise tier gets verified third-party storage support, which is absent from the tiers below it.
Media Composer First, the free entry-level tier, is also being expanded for students and beginner editors. Details have not yet been released.

Ready to Edit is a new agentic feature that automates content preparation before editing begins. The connection between Media Composer and Avid Content Core is also getting tighter. A new Content Core panel lets users import and publish assets without leaving Media Composer.

There are also updates shared across the Standard, Ultimate and Enterprise tiers. PhraseFindAI Multicam Auto Cut picks multicam angles based on who is speaking and places cuts at pauses in speech. Transcript Tools gained undo for transcript edits, segment splitting, and continuous playback in the viewer. The OpenTimelineIO 2.0 adapter improves accuracy when moving between third-party tools. A new What's New window links out to documentation and learning materials.
Also added: Bin Column Search, audio track replacement for subclips, Titler+ keyframe correction, and expanded APIs for automation and integration.

At IBC, there's also a first preview of a browser-based Media Composer workflow, starting from web editing in Avid Content Core. It could be a fairly big change for Avid editors. A new embedded AI preview, powered by a Google Gemini panel, is being unveiled alongside it.
Software developer Sebastian Beyer has released Scantic, an iPhone app that creates 3D Gaussian splats of objects and spaces using nothing but ordinary phone camera footage.

Training takes “under a minute.” Unusually for this kind of app, processing happens entirely on the phone: scan data is never uploaded to the cloud. The basic app is free, and higher-quality export modes are unlocked with payment.

3D Gaussian splatting reconstructs real objects from images or video into a fast-rendering, high-quality 3D representation. Scantic works the same way as other tools: once a scan starts, circling the subject while filming generates a splat from the captured images. A small scan takes “under a minute” to process, and the result can be exported in PLY format for use in DCC apps that support 3DGS.

CG Channel has also covered mobile 3D scanning apps like Kiri Engine and Polycam. Both have more features and include tools for trimming and editing scan data. What sets Scantic apart is that processing finishes entirely on the user's phone, avoiding security concerns and cutting out a time-consuming step. Beyer says that by the time other apps finish uploading data, Scantic has already finished training the splat.

Beyer's background is in software engineering, not CG art — he uses Blender for personal projects. Scantic grew out of a self-assigned summer project: using AI coding tools, without being a 3DGS expert, to speed up an existing 3D Gaussian splatting workflow.

The first splat he made from iPhone footage using the open-source Brush engine took more than three hours to train on a MacBook Air. With help from the Claude Fable 5 model, he steadily improved performance, eventually reaching up to 260 times faster. He then gradually moved the pipeline onto the iPhone. It became an iPhone-only app “almost by accident.”

Going forward, he plans to let splats train from existing footage rather than just live capture, and to add SPZ format export. A macOS companion app is possible, but there are no plans for an Android version. “Apple's hardware range is relatively controlled,” he says. “On Android, it would only run well on some high-end devices, and the experience would be poor on the rest.”

Scantic requires iOS 17.0 or later and an A12 Bionic chip or newer, meaning it runs on the iPhone XS from 2018 onward. The free basic app unlocks standard-quality export, which produces a thinned-down, lower-resolution version of the scan. The highest-quality export requires a subscription of 29.99 euros (about $35) per year. Exporting a single scan at the highest quality is also possible, at 4.99 euros per scan.
Netflix has released the official trailer for a bizarre reality competition series based on Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory.

The title is Wonka's The Golden Ticket. It's a nine-episode unscripted series in which contestants wander a colorful 'factory' and compete in challenges drawn from Roald Dahl's original novel. Netflix acquired the Roald Dahl Story Company in 2021.

In the trailer, contestants cheerfully endure all kinds of chaos, led by the voice of the late actor Gene Wilder — the actor who played Willy Wonka in the 1971 film. Netflix and production company Eureka Productions revived the voice with AI company ElevenLabs, with permission from Wilder's family. It's not an entirely comfortable choice, and some may find it disrespectful or, worse, unsettling.

The official description reads: “Twelve lucky Golden Ticket winners, each with a partner of their choosing, step through the doors of Wonka's chocolate factory into a world of pure imagination, sweet mischief, and unexpected challenges. Once inside, contestants must navigate Wonka's games, trials, and temptations, designed to test their strength, intellect, and morality. In this high-stakes social experiment, contestants adapt, strategize, and endure the unknown as they move through the factory's wondrous and unpredictable landscape. They must prove the intuition, resilience, and character needed to survive the chaos. Only the one who remains at the end wins Wonka's life-changing prize.”

Regarding the use of the voice, Gene Wilder's wife, Karen B. Wilder, released a statement on behalf of his estate. “It's been over fifty years since Gene brought Willy Wonka to life, yet people around the world, of every age and background, still find joy, laughter and inspiration in his performance. Gene had a singular gift for bringing humor, wonder and heart into people's lives, and that connection has carried across generations. We're delighted that Wonka's The Golden Ticket honors the warmth and imagination he brought to the role, passing that magic on to a new generation while also paying tribute to the fans who have treasured it for decades.”
Alongside the revived voice, Rusty Goffe, who played an Oompa Loompa in the 1971 film, also appears.
Chris Culvenor, Paul Franklin, Rikki Proost, David Tibballs, Allison Holloway and Emer Harkin serve as executive producers. It premieres September 23.

Wuxi, Jiangsu province, in eastern China. On Chen Hao's aging desktop, more than ten versions of Nuke, the VFX industry's standard tool, are still installed. For nearly a decade he learned each new version, and taught himself English to learn Autodesk Maya and Unreal Engine.

blocks.cap: Qidian Interactive, Wuxi's AI video studio

blocks.x: He's now technical director at Qidian Interactive, a new AI video studio in Wuxi. The platform he's building compresses that accumulated expertise into a few lines of prompt.

By around last year, AI video had become comparable to output that used to take him days to produce. The arrival of ByteDance's text-to-video model Seedance 2.0 made it much easier to turn out studio-grade footage, and the company pushed harder into AI. Chen Hao was assigned to develop its in-house model.
"I don't like AI. But I had no choice but to use it," he told Sixth Tone. "Once I realized a single click could sometimes beat two or three days of work, there was no way not to use it."

The system is called Yudian. Work began in April, and the first version shipped about a month later. It watches trending material on social media to suggest premises, writes dialogue, builds storyboards, places characters and objects in 3D space, and even judges whether an ending's cliffhanger is sharp enough to hook viewers.

A production prompt shown on one screen read: "45 to 60 seconds. Setting: a watch repair shop. Barton lunges for the pocket watch, Eliza twists her wrist to shatter the central gear. The action should be extremely fast and explosive, giving the audience no room to breathe." Camera, lens, and lighting were all specified.

Ma Shuan, a lighting artist with nearly two decades in film, including VFX work on The Wandering Earth, uses AI at Qidian to clean up live-action footage — erasing modern concrete that crept into an ancient battlefield scene, for instance. Frame-by-frame cleanup that used to take two or three days now takes half a day. "For me, AI is only an aid. Traditional production is controllable. With AI, every single result is a gamble."

In the industry, that gamble is called "card-pulling." Some studios keep a "card operator" whose only job is to keep generating until a usable shot comes out. Huang, 26, who works at a production company in Shanghai, spends his day running the same shot three or four times over. "A sofa that seats one in one cut comes back as a two-seater in the next."

Qidian's Wuxi production base opened in April. It hired more than 50 staff within a month, nearly half of them newcomers. In June, it was turning out four or five short dramas a day, each with 30 to 44 episodes. A fantasy adventure that had cleared censorship review but had been shelved because it needed a budget of 8 million to 10 million yuan ($1.19 million to $1.49 million) over three years was finished with AI in two months for roughly 1 million yuan.

As speed picked up, review work grew. Project director Chen Jie used to look at 20 shots a week; now she looks at dozens, sometimes hundreds, a day. "The footage comes out so fast it wears you down. I've become almost numb to it by now." AI-generated characters still have a "waxy" look.

Chen Hao thinks feature films are still hard to replace with AI. But he believes that once a single sentence can produce a finished 10-minute, or even 90-minute, video, many of the jobs that make up production today will simply become unnecessary. Qidian plans to license Yudian to other studios.
Two unidentified AI video models have shown up in Artificial Analysis Arena's blind test, under the code names Polaris and Vega. No one has confirmed who made them yet.

There's no official attribution. But based on the timing and the quality of the output, the host guesses one of them is likely the video model Meta has been teasing for a long time. It could be Kling 4, or it could be from somewhere nobody expected. Brent Lynch was the first to spot and post about the two models.

The video breaks down the outputs released so far, one by one, covering character consistency across multiple shots, physics, on-screen text, native audio, and even a completely uncensored baby Batman. At the end, it answers which one it would pick in a head-to-head matchup.

The Polaris tests run through a sweating pilot, a dog wrestling with physics, banner text, and a rock climber. Vega passes through a hall of mirrors and speaks Italian, but runs into trouble with text. The pilot-versus-pilot comparison becomes the deciding factor.
The second half covers StillsLab, a free shot reference library built around how AI filmmakers actually work, with each still carrying a color palette with hex codes and camera and lens information.

The feature the host singles out as something they haven't seen anywhere else is visual search: feed in your own AI-generated output, and it finds real film shots in the same visual family. It also shows a workflow of uploading screenshots to a Flora canvas and chaining them with prompts. The price really is free.

A game developer and director of RIFT, who has described himself as skeptical of generative AI, teamed up with Nura Studios to turn his retro game into ten vertical shorts releasing one per day. They were made on the Showcraft platform with a locked model trained only on his own assets. They can be watched on TikTok, YouTube Shorts, and Instagram.

An AI-assisted animated microseries has been attached to Astro Burn, a retro pixel-art game made without any AI at all. The first of ten one-minute vertical episodes went live today, with one more posting each day for ten days on TikTok, YouTube Shorts, and Instagram.

Game developer, director, and producer HaZ Dulull made the animated feature RIFT and Max Beyond, and has handled cinematics for games like Dune Awakening. This time, together with Nura Studios, he rebuilt the game's characters and world as vertical shorts. Production took place on Showcraft, an AI-assisted content creation platform Nura released this past April. It follows Rainbow Hollow, a stop-motion-style series the same platform released earlier this month.

Dulull went into this project skeptical of generative AI. His condition was that the game's identity be preserved. “Showcraft is designed for producers and creators like me who care deeply about their own IP,” Dulull said. “I wanted full control over a locked model trained only on my own assets, so that ASTROBURN's visual identity would hold up to the very end.”

Dulull served as showrunner and producer, while Nura Studios writer and director Abe Scheuermann finished the script, animation, sound design, voice recording, music, cleanup, and final delivery for each episode in about a week of working days.
Here's the teaser.

Every spot calling for acting used a human. Graziela Larroca voiced Astro, Elvis Deane voiced AL, and Brian Ulrich played several supporting roles in rotation. The music was written by a human composer, licensed through Epidemic Sound, and edited to picture.

“I much prefer human voice actors. They bring nuance to a performance that AI-generated voices rarely have,” Scheuermann said. “Same with music,” Dulull added. “AI won't tell your story for you. That's your job. This worked because the technology supported a clear creative vision, not because we threw random ideas or prompts at it and pulled out random shots.”
“Microseries are a powerful way for indie developers to promote their game where players already spend their time,” said Isabelle Riva, executive producer and VP of content at Nura Studios.

Astro Burn is a 'cute 'em up' developed by Dulull's game studio Beyond the Pixels and published by Pixel Doors. It came out on PC and Mac via Steam and GOG this past July, with mobile and console ports in the works.

New York-based Italian director Francesco Carrozzini is bringing “Be Brave” to the Venice Film Festival. It is an 85-minute portrait of Renzo Rosso, the founder of Diesel. He says he used AI in a way that “can still live inside a place for emotion and story.”

In the film, Rosso is a visionary and underdog who went against the grain, a man who rose from poverty to build a fashion empire. Yet Carrozzini never filmed his subject for a single frame. Every era of Rosso was recreated entirely with AI.

Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera, announcing the invitation, said, “I want to offer this film as an invitation to think together about what new creative possibilities AI as a tool can open up for filmmakers.” It counts among the first AI features to premiere at a top-tier festival.

The Lido is no stranger to Carrozzini. He first came with “Franca: Chaos and Creation,” about his mother, the influential editor-in-chief of Vogue Italia, and returned in 2022 with his first narrative feature, “Hanging Sun.”

Production took a year and a half. “AI changed so much in the meantime that we had to redo what we'd done early on,” he adds. “By the time it screens in theaters, it will probably already be old.” Still, he says, “it's genuinely exciting to work with a medium that changes at this speed.” The film was produced by Lorenzo Mieli, Mario Zanani and Gabriele Immirzi at Rome's Our Films.

It started out of necessity. Rosso has a large TV archive, but no usable interviews and even less of his private moments. That led to the idea of building it from scratch, even while worrying no one would believe it. From there, the idea spread into making AI itself the subject of the film.

The whole documentary is scripted. It uses a device in which the director goes looking for Rosso and Rosso evades and runs from him, and that chase became the theme itself. “This film isn't a thesis on AI. If it says one thing in the end, it's that people have to come first.”

The work itself “was a nightmare at first.” AI does not give you exactly what you ask for. As he puts it precisely, “it always gives you some version of what you requested.” Building faces from period photos, creating voices for each age, and matching lip-sync became a tedious, repetitive grind.
The hardest part was neither the face nor the voice. It was behavior. “You can get the voice perfectly. You can match the image too. But what's really hard is behavior.”

Labeling all the generated material like real footage so editors could pull from it was also a job in itself. Much of it was handled by Blackstone, with AI artist Roberto Veragnoli doing the heavy lifting. “It looks like a plain documentary. But the labor behind it is closer to a heavy CGI blockbuster.” The process of making things at low resolution and then upscaling went on continuously.

Whether audiences notice isn't his concern. What matters is making it funny and relatable. But he draws a clear line: for now, he won't take on contemporary fiction or period drama made without actors, because emotion comes from the work of real people.

Nice Touch has released V2 of its namesake app, an AI editing assistant for professional video post teams. This isn't a touch-up; it's a complete rebuild, and more than 300 conversations with editors, producers, production supervisors and studio heads shaped the design. It's available to use right now.

Here's how it works. It analyzes project footage, transcribing with word-level accuracy while separating speakers. From there you just give instructions in plain language. Say what cut you want, and the app lays actual clips, cuts and markers onto the timeline — in a state you can keep working on directly.
Starting with what's new in V2: first, where it lives has changed. It now runs inside Adobe Premiere and DaVinci Resolve.

The editing engine was also rebuilt. Interviews, podcasts, panels, direct-to-camera pieces, sessions with overlapping speakers — each has its own character. V2 reads what kind of material it has received and what kind of edit was requested, and handles it accordingly.
Multicam starts from the original multicam. Angle sync holds through any number of versions and revisions. Analysis and transcription run in 18 languages.
It's a conversation, not a black box. Editors give instructions in words, see a preview of what the app intends to do, and can put the brakes on before it runs.

The founders are Matthew Cooksey and Paul Simon. Over 12 years, the two grew Circus Street's video production outfit to 200 people and made TV- and VFX-grade content for Coca-Cola, Nike, Nestlé and Pfizer. Cooksey built a £500,000 virtual studio that produced 60 hours of content in 20 languages, reaching more than 500,000 viewers.

Media Composer, Final Cut, Premiere, Resolve — tools have changed how each generation works, but no one ever touched the most painful part. When a drive full of footage arrives, always more than expected, someone still has to watch all of it, pull selects, sync multicam and lay down an assembly. Creative judgment only begins after that. It usually eats an entire day.

Two things kept coming up across the 300 conversations. One: most existing AI tools required stepping out of editing to process something elsewhere and bring the result back in — a line editors didn't want to cross.

Two: there was no single output everyone wanted. Needs differed by project and by corner of the industry — stringouts, selects, assemblies, supercuts, cutdowns, sound bites, paper edits, each with its own precise set of expectations. V2 was built to target that range, not a single fixed output.

Pricing is on nicetouch.app. The five-day free trial unlocks every feature with 2,000 credits. Paid tiers are the 7,000-credit Pro at $67.75 a month and the 40,000-credit Ultra at $338.67 a month, with pay-as-you-go top-ups also available. Podimo and the University of Georgia's School of Social Work editing team are already using it.

Eddie AI just made its broadest overhaul since v3. The biggest change isn't a feature. The subscription is gone. This assistant editor now runs on pay-as-you-go credits, opens its entire toolset to Claude and ChatGPT through an MCP server, and fits in your pocket with a native iPhone app.

Pricing, access, and output all changed at once. The company says costs are roughly 50% lower under the new credit model. There are about 100 MCP tools, covering transcripts, soundbites, assembly, b-roll, captions, music, voiceover, multicam angles, and NLE export. A single chat window directs the edit. The company is showing all of this at IBC 2026 in Amsterdam.

What changed the structure is pricing. Subscription tiers used to sit alongside credit options, but that structure is gone. The pricing page now has only credit packs: 1,000 credits for $10, 5,000 credits for $45, 15,000 credits for $120, 50,000 credits for $350, and custom pricing above that. Credits don't expire and unlock every feature regardless of pack size. Auto-reload is optional and off by default.

Credits are charged for everything the system does. Importing footage costs around 500 credits per hour of source material, billed in 15-minute increments. Running an edit varies in cost by workload, and large jobs show an estimated cost before you run them. New accounts start with 1,000 free credits, enough to take one small project from import to export without spending anything.

The second shift is distribution. With Eddie AI running as an MCP server, the Claude or ChatGPT window an editor already has open can drive the edit directly. Describe the cut you want in the chat, and it runs against footage already uploaded to the cloud.

Inside ChatGPT, results come back as playback cards built from actual frames rather than links. The language model never touches the media. It plans and instructs, while Eddie AI holds the footage, timecodes, and timeline. The export path to editors finishing in Premiere Pro, DaVinci Resolve, or Final Cut Pro stays the same. You hand off the timeline, and a human does the finishing.

blocks.cap: The Eddie AI app. Source: Eddie AI

blocks.x: The iPhone app is a free download on the App Store, requiring iOS 15.1 or later. Its scope is deliberately narrow: you prompt an edit, review the finished cut, and either save the MP4 or share a link that opens without an account. The company is clear that this isn't a mobile editing tool. The heavy media stays in the cloud, and the app handles review and direction.

The collaboration layer was also rebuilt. Projects sync in real time across web, desktop, and phone. Workspaces share team membership and a credit pool, and comments pin to an exact frame and go straight to the editor. Slack and Microsoft Teams integration and enterprise SSO are in now too.

It also generates material your shoot didn't capture. Audio covers original music, voiceover in a chosen voice, and dubbing tracks layered onto an existing edit, with automatic mixing. On the visual side, you can describe the shot you want in words to pull it from stock and drop it on the timeline, or generate b-roll outright. All of it is optional, and all of it is billed. Eddie AI repeats the same line here too: it doesn't invent your footage.
Core features of the AI-based VFX platform Slapshot — things like automatic rotoscoping and camera tracking — are now available as nodes inside Comfy, the environment for building AI pipelines.

blocks.x: CG Channel tries to cover the big CG software updates that come out every week, but smaller updates and worthwhile plugins sometimes slip through. To avoid letting them go unnoticed, we've gathered game, VFX, and motion graphics tool news from last week that didn't get a standalone story. Below are the 3D Gaussian splatting app Postshot, the generative modeling tool Meshy, and AI VFX tools from Slapshot and Topaz Labs.

Hyperion 2.5. Topaz Labs has updated its AI model for converting SDR to HDR, which moves 8-bit footage to 10-bit or 16-bit. Color processing, tonal separation, highlight detail, and overall sharpness have improved, and the color and luminance range is wider. Hyperion is used in the desktop app Topaz Video and the web app Astra, but 2.5 has so far only rolled out to Astra. Astra subscriptions start at $39 a month or $328 a year.

Meshy 7. The generative AI model that creates 3D models from source images has moved to its seventh generation, improving the quality of models the web app produces. Overall proportions, the relative position of parts, and preservation of fine surface detail are all better. A commercial subscription is $20 a month, and studio is $70 a month. The free plan generates up to 10 models a month under a Creative Commons license.

Postshot 1.1.69. The scanning app that turns photographic stills or video into 3D Gaussian splats has refined its workflow a year after its commercial launch. New additions include an HTML export option, an SPZ export quality option, SPZ 4 support, an option to attach GPS location metadata to cameras and points, and point cloud import without color attributes. Non-commercial use is free, the indie subscription is €26 a month or €204 a year, and studio is €59 a month. It only supports Windows 10 or later.

New Slapshot Comfy nodes. Slapshot's tools for pulling VFX assets from source footage — rotoscoping, camera tracking, motion vectors, and depth map generation — now run as nodes inside the Comfy interface for building generative AI workflows. The free Slapshot plan is limited to 2K sources, and commercial subscriptions start at $9 a month. The new Comfy nodes charge $0.25 per video frame processed. Comfy Desktop itself is a free download and runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
The University of Southern California's Entertainment Technology Center has brought Beeble's AI production tools into film education.
Through the partnership, ETC students get hands-on experience with AI workflows in visual effects, virtual production, and cinematic storytelling.

ETC is a think tank inside USC's School of Cinematic Arts. It has worked with major studios, technology companies, and filmmakers to validate new technologies and refine future production practices. It announced that it has now added Beeble to its film production research and practicum courses.

Beeble has found a place across several programs. These include “Introduction to Practical Effects for Film,” led by Habib Zargarpour; “Directing with AI,” led by Fred Grinstein; and experimental film work in USC's Media Arts + Practice program, which includes Amazon-supported research and PhD work.

“Visual effects workflows keep changing. It's important for students to understand both established production techniques and the emerging technologies that are shaking up the industry. Bringing tools like Beeble into the classroom becomes valuable hands-on experience,” said Erik Weaver, ETC's head of AI and emergent media.

“One of the most rewarding outcomes is seeing students actually push ideas that would have once been beyond the scope of a class assignment,” said Tom Thudiyanplackal, producer and industry mentor at ETC. “They could dream about visual effects at this scale, but rarely got the chance to build them. Putting these kinds of tools in their hands opens up entirely new creative paths.”

The collaboration also extends into production research outside the classroom. One example is “Pathways,” written and directed by Felipe Vargas and shot by Roberto Schaefer, which explores new approaches to virtual production, cinematography, and AI-assisted world-building.

“ETC plays the role of bringing educators, filmmakers, and industry together to validate emerging technologies,” said Beeble CEO Hoon Kim. “It's genuinely rewarding to see our tools used in that environment and contribute to how future production workflows will take shape.”

In the thoroughly analog setting of a federal courthouse in San Jose, one of the strangest — and potentially most consequential — fights over who truly owns what in the AI age is heading toward a resolution. Slop, trademark and copyright claims, Italian brainrot memes and licensing disputes are all tangled together, with Tung Tung Sahur at the center. Roblox and Fortnite make supporting appearances.

blocks.cap: Tung Tung Sahur / San Jose Federal Courthouse

blocks.x: A hearing is set for September 23 before Judge Noël Wise. Plaintiffs Spider Games and Speedy Simulator Gaming, and defendant-turned-countersuing Momentum Labs, are each asking the court to dismiss the other's claims.

It started with one very low-tech email. In mid-2025, France-based Momentum reached out to Two Big Studios, owned by Spider Games, with a complaint: Tung Tung Sahur was appearing in “Steal a Brainrot,” their hit Roblox gathering-and-hunting game.

Momentum had licensed Tung Tung Sahur from Indonesian creator Noksa (real name Fernanda Vagas Indrastata) — the character with legs made of a wooden stick, a blank smile and a baseball bat. Having already struck a deal with Epic Games' Fortnite, Momentum sought the same from Two Big Studios.
It looks like an ordinary IP negotiation — a few emails, some back-and-forth, a Zoom call or two with lawyers, a handful of payments, and it's done. Not this time.

Roblox, already unpopular with parents and teachers, briefly pulled Tung Tung Sahur, handing Momentum a short-lived win. But as soon as negotiations stalled, Spider preemptively sued Momentum. The U.S. Copyright Office has said AI-generated works can be protected, but on a case-by-case basis, and Momentum did not have full U.S. copyright secured when the dispute began.

Steven Stein, Momentum's outside counsel, put it this way: “This case is one front in a global fight that touches a bigger question — can a company commercialize human-made creative work without permission or compensation, simply because AI was involved?” He adds, briefly, “We don't think so.”

The other side's logic is simpler. Mitchell Silberberg & Knupp, representing the “Steal a Brainrot” team, stated flatly in a July 30 amended complaint: “The rights Momentum claims do not exist. Under established law, copyright protection requires human authorship, and AI-generated works do not qualify.” Momentum filed a trademark infringement counterclaim the same day and, on August 19, moved to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction.

MSK's Aaron Moss told Deadline: “This dispute began when Momentum sent cease-and-desist letters to my clients. Momentum claims to own dozens of ‘Italian brainrot’ memes and casts itself as their ‘commercial gatekeeper.' But no one — not Momentum, not anyone — owns brainrot, because it's all AI-generated content.”

Trial is set for November 29, 2027. Whichever way the September hearing tips, some of the dice will already be cast on how much human involvement AI-generated content needs. It will also start to show whether what studios, streamers, YouTube and the creator economy have treated as solid assets is actually solid — or full of holes.

The closing follows the usual order: a best AI tools guide and a free compliance guide, followed by community news, then the AI film of the week starting at 26:00 — Adam Palmer's Primer AI spec ad, Danny Tseng's The Tower, and Dave Clark's Plume.

The future we usually get to see is one that's falling apart: ruined cities, bleak endings, a signal to brace yourself. befores & afters calls this a failure of imagination, because the future we picture ends up being the future we build.
So the Future Vision XPRIZE asked for the opposite. Three minutes. Any tool. No professional résumé required. 6,000 people have made one.

blocks.cap: The Future Vision XPRIZE finalist screening takes place on September 25th in downtown LA

blocks.x: Live action, animation, generative, or all three in a single shot. By not restricting the toolset, the entries give a fairly honest picture of what people are actually reaching for right now, and how much the gap has closed between what a small team can pull off and what used to require a full facility.

Ten of them made the finals. They'll take the stage on September 25th at a restored 1920s movie palace in downtown LA to present in person. The winner walks away with a $2.5 million production grant to develop into a real film with Range Media Partners, with a budget that can run up to $15 million. The four runners-up get $100,000 each. Judges include Neal Stephenson and Neil deGrasse Tyson.

There's one more award that same night. $2 million goes to a founder who used AI over 90 days to solve a real problem people actually face. Judges are Palmer Luckey, Cathie Wood, Anousheh Ansari, Mark Pincus, and Logan Kilpatrick. More than 30,000 people competed for the two awards.

$5.5 million gets decided that night, in that room, in front of everyone. No pre-recording, no envelopes opened in advance. Capacity is 1,500 seats. Peter Diamandis hosts, with Google, Circle, and XPRIZE co-presenting.

The debate over open-weight models caught fire when 35 organizations, including Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Hugging Face, signed the “Open-Weights and American AI Leadership” open letter. The argument is that models anyone can download, inspect, modify, and run on their own infrastructure form one pillar of the foundation.

blocks.cap: An image generated locally with the open diffusion transformer Z-Image-turbo, via fxguide. Credit: Jack Higgins

blocks.x: fxguide points out that the situation on the ground in VFX isn't that simple. Running the latest open-source GenAI workflows in-house is itself a security hole. ComfyUI is a great tool, but its code and open plugin ecosystem leave room for malware to slip in, and there's too much code for an in-house IT team to audit all of it. GPU shortages and spiking RAM prices still keep mid-sized companies tied to the cloud.

fxguide also ran a piece by JD Vandenberg, a GenAI workflow and color science consultant who has worked with Disney and Netflix. His summary is that bringing in open-weight models comes with workflow stability, security, predictable costs, and delivery efficiency.

During production, software doesn't get updated unless it absolutely has to be. GenAI models, by contrast, change often, with no warning and no published changelog. The same input with the same seed can produce different results. Tools can disappear overnight. In March, when OpenAI shut down the Sora app and web service, Critterz missed its planned Cannes unveiling, and its co-creators had to find a new AI partner and reschedule for early 2027.

blocks.cap: A watercolor-style image made locally the same way. Credit: Jack Higgins

blocks.x: Security is more straightforward. Production networks keep the paths leading outward narrow under MPA and TPN content security requirements, but the moment you send source material to a hosted model and get results back, you've punched a hole in that perimeter. What travels through that hole is usually unreleased assets. On-premises models can run even on a fully closed network.

Costs are hard to predict. Patrick Cederberg, post supervisor at the Toronto collective Shy Kids, which made the 2024 Sora short Air Head, told fxguide that getting to a finished 90 seconds took “hundreds of generations at 10 to 20 seconds each,” putting the ratio of source to final cut at around 300:1. Scripted shoots usually run between 10:1 and 30:1. As of August 2026, API rates run $0.05 to $0.75 per second of output, so the cost of one finished minute multiplies the per-second price by a factor that's hard to pin down. In June, one employee at a San Francisco fintech burned through $81,267 worth of tokens in a week while building a game.

The hardware is already on hand. Today's video models often ship distilled, quantized versions that run on a single workstation GPU. Render farm and color grading GPUs also sit idle outside work hours. But open-weight and open-source aren't the same thing. Being able to download weights is separate from being allowed to fine-tune, redistribute, or deliver commercially, and licenses range from Apache 2.0 to noncommercial-only. No matter how good the result looks, discovering a license blocks commercial use at the confirmation stage is already too late.

Adobe has shipped a Photoshop update. It's a bundle that lines up precision tools and prompt-based editing side by side and lets you pick either. Leading the pack: a new Light Adjustment Layer, Instruct Edit with Masks powered by Firefly, and the beta AI Assisted Editor.

blocks.cap: A screen from the beta AI Assisted Editor

blocks.x: Deepa Subramaniam, VP of product marketing for creative pros, said in the announcement: “Whether you're refining details with precision tools or exploring ideas with prompts, this update is built to help you work more efficiently and confidently while staying focused on your creative vision from start to finish.”

The Light Adjustment Layer packs exposure, contrast, highlights, shadows, whites, and blacks into a single non-destructive adjustment layer, producing Camera Raw-level results without ever leaving your layer workflow.

With Instruct Edit with Masks, Firefly Image 5 reads the full context of an image. Instead of pointing out exactly where to edit, you can just say, in a sentence, to open a closed eye or put a hat on a specific person's head. Everything outside the mask is left untouched, so faces, logos, and brand assets stay intact. The new Markup feature lets you draw directly on the image to show what you mean: paint the area you want recolored, draw an arrow for placement, and rough-brush in new elements. It cuts down on the ambiguity that comes from describing everything in words alone.

blocks.cap: An example of an Instruct Edit job with a mask applied

blocks.x: Dynamic Text, Shapes and Paths extends Photoshop's dynamic text to custom shapes and paths, so letters automatically sit along a curve or a free-form layout. Stock Panel Integration brings more than 900 million Adobe Stock assets into a docked panel inside Photoshop.

The beta AI Assisted Editor is a separate interface with a natural-language prompt bar. Using it is optional. It bundles Prompt to Edit, Remove Background, Generative Expand, Remove Tool, Generative Fill, Generative Upscale, and AI Markup.

For those who stay in the Pro Editor, Prompt to Edit has also landed in the Contextual Task Bar. Without making a selection, a single prompt line can change the whole image, and each result stacks into the layer panel as a new generative layer. The update is available in Photoshop now.

Silicon Valley's “move fast and break things” sounds plausible for innovation. It can't be aimed at the very fabric of society. In the middle of a technological revolution, it's time for lawmakers to recognize that risk.

Art is a process before it's an output. Keeping the spark of inspiration alive happens within that process. It can start from talent. But it only becomes an expression that could come from no one else's experience once diligence, discipline, patience, and persistence attach to it. “Reducing art to a 'prompt' is an insult to every creator, past, present, and future.”

The author is David Barber, president of MPSE (Motion Picture Sound Editors). He insists that the people who've staked their lives on this work must be protected, and that legislation is the way to do it.

Let's draw a line first. Prompt-generated output means cases where an AI engine, not a human author, creates the expressive details — video, audio, music, scripts, or images produced from natural-language input or video-to-sound. That's different from tools that refine material a person already made.

The proposal has two provisions. First, deny copyright to generative AI's prompt-based output, and to any whole work that incorporates even part of it. Second, require labeling on the output and its derivatives: visible for pictures and video, audible for songs, scores, and sound effects, and traceable through metadata.

The scope isn't narrow. It covers films that use a prompt-made score, sound effects, visual effects, or voiceover. The same goes for a song if a prompt-generated horn section or backing vocals contributed to finishing the track. Companies hiding behind trade secret law also need to be blocked.

He grounds it in law too. US federal statute defines a copyrighted work as “an original work of authorship fixed in a tangible medium of expression.” Originality is recognized when a human author creates something independently with at least a minimal degree of creativity — the “spark” and “minimal” the Supreme Court invoked in Feist Publications v. Rural Telephone Service.

Barber's judgment is firm. A machine that assembles massive datasets at the fastest speed in human history is a marvel of innovation, not an artist. Prompt-based output is ultimately math, and there's no spark of creativity in it.

Asked whether the Copyright Office already holds this position, he says not exactly. Exceptions like “substantial human editing” or “creative selection and arrangement” leave the door open. Pull one thread and a hole opens that can't be closed.

One case has already slipped through. The Copyright Office, after a reconsideration process, granted copyright to “A Single Piece of American Cheese,” made by Invoke AI CEO Kent Keirsey. The company's own description is blunt: “We weren't trying to make a masterpiece (obviously). We wanted to see where the floor is for the US Copyright Office granting copyright to AI-assisted work.”

Tens of thousands of AI-made “songs” go up on Spotify every day, and some chart. Because payouts are divided by stream count, that much more comes out of human artists' share. He calls output that doesn't disclose its training data “fruit of the poison tree.” “How much do you have to modify a stolen car before it becomes yours to sell?”

Once a single song gets trained on, the shares of the producer, songwriter, engineer, mixer, and performers all get pulled in whole. Film is worse: writers, cinematographers, production designers, editors, sound editors, Foley artists, even VFX artists. The piece ends with one line aimed at Congress: “Which of you will become the champion of human creativity?”

blocks.cap: After Effects Portal August 2026 · ProVideo Coalition

blocks.x: This is Rich Young's monthly After Effects roundup. The first half of this year has been a rush of major features, AI and premium competition, and third-party news. The current stable release is 26.3, from the June 2026 release.

26.3 added depth of field for the Advanced 3D Renderer, copy-paste for Illustrator/SVG content, a reworked mask tracker, frame clipboard copy, a Curl Noise effect that wraps 2D patterns, variable font finding by axis, and the Frame.io V4 panel.

With IBC and Adobe MAX coming up, the beta side is busy. The After Effects AI Assistant, editable text imported from Illustrator files, a new guides feature, Object Matte disk caching, Contour Paint, Alt/Option-drag layer duplication, anchor point changes, a modernized Effect Controls panel, and effect color labels are all on the beta list.

Looking at the long run, the AI Assistant is the biggest one. Instead of following menus, you describe what you want to do in words, and it asks follow-up questions to refine it. The assistant turns that request into actions inside the project and composition. Right now it can organize projects, work on expressions, and generate images and video. SternFX and flomotion each posted introduction videos.

Attempts to attach AI to AE aren't limited to Adobe. Atom and the Claude/Higgsfield extension are the notable examples, and Davey Design says it made the first AI agent for After Effects. Jake Bartlett has good things to say about Atom, but there's no comparison yet with Adobe's version.

There's free-tier news too. Jake In Motion's free panel Code Runner 2 bundles scripts, expressions, presets, menu commands, and keyframe easing into a single button. Caddis 1.0.5 supports Linux and MCP and offers a 7-day trial. Maxon is pushing people to start with Autograph for free, and Cavalry, which Canva acquired, has also gone free.

404 Media talked with Hany Farid about the future of deepfakes. Farid is a co-founder of the AI image detection company GetReal, and the person who created PhotoDNA, the perceptual hashing algorithm now used by every major platform.

Real-time generation is already within reach. But will every pixel really be generated, as Jensen Huang puts it? The people standing in the middle each want to skim off a little money, but Rich Young's counter-question is that there's no reason most of the work couldn't be done locally. If you want to be a utility, you also have to be ready for regulation.

Gal Gadot appeared on the podcast “Happy Sad Confused” to promote the Prime Video action movie “The Runner.” When host Josh Horowitz brought up a third Wonder Woman movie, she said she doesn't think she'd go back to it now.

“I think about what it would be like to do Wonder Woman one more time, but with four kids and different schools, I don't have the confidence in my current life. Being away from my kids that long doesn't fit my life anymore.”

Gadot played Wonder Woman in Zack Snyder's DC Universe. She first appeared in 2016's “Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice,” and Patty Jenkins' 2017 “Wonder Woman” made $824 million worldwide. She went through “Justice League” that same year, then reunited with Jenkins on 2020's “Wonder Woman 1984.”

Around the time Jenkins was developing “Wonder Woman 3,” James Gunn and Peter Safran took over DC Studios and the Snyder era effectively ended. Gadot said in 2023 that a third film would be developed in the rebooted DC Universe, but Variety sources at the time said Gunn and Safran had no intention of continuing a Gadot-led sequel. Gadot wasn't surprised when she got the notice that she was out.

“I saw how everyone else got wrapped up. Henry's (Cavill's) ending is hard to call graceful. Same with Patty's (Jenkins's). We're all adults and everyone's fine. I'm grateful for the chance to have worn these boots and watched the character be loved that much. I hope the next person comes into this journey with a pure heart. This character means a lot to a lot of people. It was never mine to begin with, I was just the vessel. That's Hollywood.”

Gadot also brought up Doug Liman's upcoming film “Bitcoin.” It's a project that drew controversy for making its sets and lighting with AI. Filming with Casey Affleck, Pete Davidson, and Isla Fisher took place in an empty space with nothing in it. Producer Ryan Kavanaugh claimed the $70 million project saved over $200 million by filling in production design and lighting with AI.

“It was the longest contract I've ever worked on. The lawyers spent six months going through every possible scenario tied to AI, one by one. I wanted AI to not touch my acting. That had to be protected, and in the end, SAG asked my lawyers for advice as it worked on revising clauses to protect other actors. All the acting is me.”

“I'm scared of AI. Does that mean I'm scared and look away? No. I'm scared, but I touch it, learn it, study it. The train has already left the station. You either work with it, or you're completely out of the game. I try to use it as well as I can and protect what can be protected. On this movie, what AI handled was the sets and lighting. The team was large, and a lot of people worked hard on this movie.”
Because Liman shot the actors in what was essentially an empty warehouse, only the actors were on set. Gadot compared the experience to theater.

“It felt like a pure form of making a movie. I haven't seen a single cut yet. Actors spend a lot of time waiting. There's that famous line, ‘Acting is getting paid to wait.’ Here, there was no need to wait for lighting, so we shot nonstop. We even shot for ten hours straight sometimes. It was incredible... an actor is always warmed up, with no time to cool down. We'll have to see. It's a crazy thing.”

“At Utopai Studios, we're building a new model for filmmaking. We give creators more ways to bring ambitious ideas to the screen, while keeping their vision at the center of every production,” said Kevin Jung, COO of Utopai Studios. “The future of film is made where artistry, technology, and new production methods meet. That's why we're glad to join Variety at TIFF. We want to look at how new tools, techniques, and creative approaches are expanding what directors can do, and how those stories reach audiences.”

blocks.cap: Danny Boyle · Jacopo Salvi/La Biennale di Venezia

blocks.x: Danny Boyle voiced deep concern about the impact artificial intelligence could have on journalism and other fields. 「It's insane what we're doing.」

「Journalism is one of the great pillars that holds up any civilization,」 Boyle said at the press conference for his film 'Ink,' which opens the Venice Film Festival's competition section this evening. 「There are people who stand up and speak truth to power. It really matters that a society has people like that.」

「The danger is that big tech companies and their AI could replace journalism,」 Boyle said. 「You'll be able to have a much more efficient, much cheaper AI reporter. Will that AI reporter speak truth to the power that created it? That's going to be a very difficult and interesting question.」

Boyle said other professions, including teaching, are just as much at risk. 「Teachers are also one of the pillars that holds up our society, and teachers too could be replaced by AI. What we're doing is insane. Where is that village we all need? And within that village, there are people who speak truths that are unwelcome, and sometimes unpopular, because of what they say.」
「I want 'Ink' to raise those questions about the future, and about the place we're pushing our way into.」

Adapted from James Graham's play, the film begins in 1969. It tells the story of a rising media mogul, Rupert Murdoch, buying 'The Sun' and, with editor Larry Lamb, building it into the most influential tabloid in Britain.

「Striking the balance is really tricky,」 Graham said when asked how he thought Murdoch would see the film. 「You need to gain access in order to report, but at the same time you have to keep your independence, your integrity, and your distance.」

「He was very good at not leaking anything, and that's probably one of the secrets of his success,」 Graham continued. 「There's one thing I remember. Murdoch really enjoyed the print-setting scenes we recreated in the film. The dust and steam and grime that came off making a newspaper every day. He is a newsman. People only see him as a businessman, but he has a romance for the news.」

Guy Pearce, who like Murdoch was born in Australia, said he had been in touch with Murdoch's daughter and producer, Elisabeth Murdoch, about the casting. 「She told me, 'my father is very happy you're playing him.' I hadn't seen the film yet at that point, so it remains to be seen.」
Boyle acknowledged that 「a lot of people love 'The Sun' and a lot of people hate it,」 and said that, like the play, the film 「doesn't turn Rupert Murdoch into a monster.」

「At the time, he was like a breath of fresh air in a very rigid British society, and he faced no small amount of prejudice for being Australian. He particularly hated the British establishment, which I feel the same way about.」
「I hope the film is a lot of fun. It mattered to us that the audience feels like an accomplice who's dipped a foot into this journey with us from the very start.」
Netflix bought the U.S. and Latin America rights to 'Ink' in July, and Studiocanal is handling worldwide sales.
The Venice Film Festival runs from September 2 to 12.

Adobe Firefly news has mostly centered on agentic workflow updates lately. This time it's audio. The features for generating music, voice, and sound effects have fully launched and opened to all users. The promise of commercially safe AI audio remains intact.

blocks.cap: Adobe Firefly Audio Tools / Credit: Adobe

blocks.x: The tools themselves aren't new. But Generate Music, Generate Speech, and Generate Sound Effects have all now gone live and come together in one place within Firefly.

Generate Music uses the Firefly Music model. It creates original tracks matched to a video's length and mood. Licensing is fully cleared, so you don't have to worry about takedowns no matter where the content ends up.

Generate Speech is built on the Firefly Speech model, and you can also choose ElevenLabs voices. Enter a script and it produces clear narration, with controls for voice, pace, and emotion. Generate Sound Effects uses the Firefly Audio model to create sounds matched to action, timing, and energy.
A version of Generate Music was released more than two years ago. Since then, it has established itself as an option for pulling original tracks that are safe for commercial use.

The Firefly AI Assistant, still in beta, has also opened up for free. Its scope now extends to building storyboards for film and video projects and brand kits for marketing. Gemini Omni Flash is a new addition to the list of models available in Firefly. Google, ElevenLabs, Kling AI, Luma AI, OpenAI, Runway, and others are already on the list.

It's the Airbender Avatar story fans already know. The animation is different. Some have even said it exceeds expectations and surpasses the original, though the people who made it don't put it that way themselves. “Our team was almost entirely fans of 'Avatar: The Last Airbender.'” That's from Christian Bakel of Flying Bark Productions, who served as animation director on the feature.

'Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender' is set 13 years after the Nickelodeon series created by Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko. Flying Bark and Studio Mir handled the animation. Lauren Montgomery directed, with Steve Ahn and William Mata co-directing. It's available on Paramount+.

The original series was built on hand-drawn artwork and painted backgrounds. So Flying Bark chose an NPR (non-photorealistic rendering) approach. Working like painters within screen space, building up images layer by layer, stroke by stroke, while leaving camera movement, tracking, dynamic lighting, and temporal stability to 3D animation.

“Action is a huge part of the movie, and the fight scenes have a lot of camera rotation.” That's from CEO Barbara Stephen. “We wanted to create that dynamic space. But if even one character's clothing drifts off-model, it stands out.” Bakel added: “Dealing with a constantly moving camera while matching every subtle hand gesture, posture, and footing was a huge burden. The film's vision was so specific that there was nothing off the shelf, no program or software, we could just grab and use. It took three years to build new tools and a new pipeline to get that look.”

Digital frame-by-frame drawing was done in Toon Boom, and coloring in Photoshop. On top of that came CG software like Katana, Arnold, and Maya Blender, with final compositing finished in Nuke. “We use a lot of technology, but in the end we wanted everything to look handmade.” That's Bakel. “It felt like we'd picked out the hardest, most labor-intensive parts of both 2D animation and CG production and stitched them together.”

The team had almost no martial arts experts. Avatar Studios, which did have experts, sent over motion-capture footage so the movement in those shots could be matched to the real thing. No 2D rigs were used anywhere in this film. “Sometimes you can reuse a drawing,” Bakel said. “But most of it, we drew it all.”

The characters deal with water, fire, air, and earth — unpredictable elements. “Everyone wanted a crack at the water spirit at some point. There's just so much physics and performance to work out.” Bending was especially tricky. Unlike the physics of splashing water or a tipping bucket, it required calculating invisible forces that had to mesh precisely with a character's movement. A single shot could pass through more than 20 artists and multiple departments, and some shots traveled around for six to nine months.

Air is sometimes visible and sometimes not, so the team decided to show the flow of emotion through fabric and hair. Since everything was hand-drawn, the animators had to imagine and design the wind's direction, strength, and consistency themselves — what would sway the most, and what would settle first because of its length and weight. “It was about knowing and understanding the physics, and then figuring out where to break it so it looks better than reality and leaves a bigger emotional impact.”

Eline Van der Velden, the creator of Tilly Norwood, has called on public service broadcasters (PSBs) to increase their investment in AI. She made the remark fully aware of the negative stigma attached to the technology, saying that admitting you work with AI is a bit like admitting you have an STI.

blocks.cap: Eline Van der Velden / Source: Particle6

blocks.x: Tilly Norwood, the AI actor she created, became internationally known last year. Hollywood actors and major industry figures pushed back over this fast-growing software and its potential impact on creative fields.

Van der Velden, the Dutch-born CEO of London-based Particle6, raised a different point at the opening session of the Edinburgh TV Festival. She said she has signed “hundreds of NDAs” with companies, from U.S. studios to local indies, looking to bring AI into their pipeline. “There aren't many boardrooms we haven't been invited into.” The implication was that she knows how much AI companies are using behind the scenes.
The problem comes after that, she noted, half-jokingly. “Saying you work with AI is like saying you have an STI. Nobody wants to admit it.”

Van der Velden urged UK public broadcasters to shed the stigma and invest in training their staff on AI, arguing it's necessary to protect the country's creative capacity. “There's a massive arms race happening here. Britain was a creative powerhouse because it could make whatever it wanted.” She added that the technology should be seen not as a cost-cutting tool but as “a completely new medium.”

Joshua Barnett, CEO of After Party Studios, recently acquired by Sister Group, said he used AI for the creative deck on 'The Ultimate Football Challenge,' hosted by Jürgen Klopp. James Duncan, co-founder of ShxtsNGigs, said he's not worried about AI-made content stealing his YouTube audience, viewing it instead as additive to human creativity. The most useful niche right now, he said, is “things you physically can't do,” and he predicted an AI video of “someone doing four backflips off a mountain” wouldn't catch on with audiences.

A big piece of animation and visual effects history is being sold off this weekend in Berkeley, California. Oscar-winning animator and effects pioneer Phil Tippett is closing the studio he's run for decades, clearing out years' worth of props, models, artwork, equipment, and memorabilia.

The 6,200-square-foot Tippett Studio facility is being emptied in a three-day liquidation sale, running through Sunday. According to the sale listing, Tippett used this Berkeley space for 35 years, and “everything is going,” from stop-motion and motion-capture gear to cameras, model-making tools, and production documents. There are hundreds, maybe thousands, of items drawn from the studio's body of work.

Up for sale are models and sketches from 'Mad God,' an artist-proof AT-AT model from 'The Empire Strikes Back,' miniatures from 'Starship Troopers,' signed posters, storyboards, costumes, and prototypes. There are also three models tied to the Dejarik chess scene from the original 'Star Wars.' The full working infrastructure of the shop is included too — computers, 3D printers, lighting gear, welding equipment, a drill press, mold-making setups, and toolboxes.

Two items aren't for sale: the Oscars. Of the trophies he won for 'Return of the Jedi' and 'Jurassic Park,' the 74-year-old director told CBS San Francisco: “They're the most valuable things, and they were the most meaningful moments of my journey.” As for letting go of the rest, he admitted: “Every once in a while a little bit of regret creeps in.”

The closure marks the end of a hard period for one of the most prominent names in American visual effects. Tippett Studio agreed in 2024 to hand a majority stake to the Indian VFX company PhantomFX and filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection that May. A reorganization plan was approved in April 2025, and PhantomFX said it completed the acquisition that July.

Tippett and his wife and producing partner, Jules Roman, founded the studio in 1984. After working on the original 'Star Wars,' Tippett helped develop go-motion, an evolution of stop-motion with motion blur built in. The career-defining moment came with 'Jurassic Park.' He went in to build stop-motion dinosaur puppets, but when the production shifted to CG, he adapted along with his team. He became a bridge carrying stop-motion's knowledge and physical sensibility into the then-emerging field of CG animation, and the techniques established then shaped decades of character animation and visual effects that followed.

The studio went on to work on 'Starship Troopers,' the 'Matrix' series, 'Hellboy,' and 'Twilight.' In the meantime, Tippett worked on the stop-motion feature 'Mad God' whenever he could, premiering it at Locarno in 2021.

Closing the Berkeley space doesn't mean the Tippett Studio name disappears. PhantomFX completed its acquisition last year, and the new owner is keeping the name. What's ending is the workshop that made decades of film history. “It ran for almost 40 years. It was a good run.” He doesn't seem ready to retire just yet: “I'll die with a knife in my hand.”

blocks.cap: The Caira camera now includes generative video editing.

blocks.x: Camera Intelligence has added Generative Video Editing to the Caira app. The feature runs on Google's Gemini Omni and Runway's Aleph 2.0, and it only touches footage already shot rather than generating video from text. The private beta starts today.

The AI-native Micro Four Thirds mirrorless Caira had a somewhat rocky start. Since then, Camera Intelligence has delivered most of its Kickstarter units and asked 111 backers what they wanted built next. 77% named generative video editing.

The company says that by adding Google's Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash and Runway's Aleph 2.0, it has built the first case of a video generation model that understands real scenes placed directly into a mirrorless camera system.

The feature works in the Caira app on footage shot with Caira. Natural-language templates apply effects to the frame and camera movement. Gemini Omni was chosen because it tends to keep track of a scene's shapes, light, materials, and motion. It isn't always perfect, but the goal is to relight or widen a scene while people, objects, and camera movement stay steady throughout the clip.

The launch templates are four: Relight, Reframe, Camera Motion, and Set Extension. They range from color grading to virtual camera moves that sweep like a drone. The templates were made by Camera Intelligence with community input, and can be adjusted further with plain-English instructions. Output comes in 720p or 1080p and takes one to three minutes depending on resolution.

The company shut down an open-ended generative photo editing prompt box in March 2026. 「Vague or ridiculous」 test prompts drew backlash, so it switched to a cleaner set of buttons. How this template approach differs from that one is worth watching.

There's one notable, and perhaps welcome, clue. There is no text-to-video. Every edit starts from footage the user shot with Caira, and it cannot generate a scene out of nothing. Generated clips are saved as clearly named, separate files with Google's SynthID watermark attached, and the originals are left untouched. In-camera image processing on Caira also remains non-generative, and this feature is optional.

On safeguards, the company said that neither Camera Intelligence nor the Google API uses customers' videos and photos to train models. It also blocks changes to a person's skin color, race, or fundamental facial features.

Generative Video Editing will be part of Caira Studio, a premium software tier arriving in fall 2026. It will come bundled with Generative Image Editing and a third feature not yet announced, with pricing not yet set. It will only be available in the U.S. and the U.K. The private beta opens today to existing Caira customers and five working filmmakers, and signups go through cameraintelligence.com/generative-video-editing or team@cameraintelligence.com.
Meanwhile, the fifth batch of units is now open for preorder at $999 and will ship within the month.

blocks.cap: Eddie AI Agent Marketplace · Eddie AI

blocks.x: Eddie AI, which we've covered several times as an assistant editing tool, has launched an Agent Marketplace. Editing agents that carry the named rules of well-known editors, directors, and creators go up here.

Users can also build their own agents that follow their own rules, such as a brand book or a legal checklist. But for many, the bigger news will be the chance to work, in that specific sense, with some of the biggest names in editing and film.
This one is bound to draw comments. Here's what to know if you're interested.
As noted above, the core of this is the Agent Marketplace. Eddie AI, a feature-heavy AI assistant editing platform, is gathering agents modeled on masters of the film industry here.

One thing worth flagging: what these agents studied is the filmmakers' body of work as a whole, not the people themselves, and they have no relationship with the company. Setting that caveat aside, if you want to work with agents modeled on these masters' work, the roster includes Walter Murch, Thelma Schoonmaker, Roger Deakins, Denis Villeneuve, Ken Burns, Errol Morris, and more than twenty other names.
When an agent makes a cut, it spins up a separate new edit. It does not overwrite the edit in progress. It can also act as a critic or a second set of eyes, offering feedback on the work.

The other half of this update is the ability for users to build their own agents. This is useful if you want something that follows rules and brand guidelines set by your own team and project, rather than Christopher Nolan.

Agents are built inside the Eddie web app. You give it a name and emoji, a one-line description of what it does, and an instruction that sets its personality. Then you teach it skills, each made up of a one-line 「when to use it」 and a body of unlimited length. That body is where you upload material like brand guidelines.

One notable example is a brand-compliance agent. It scans an edit against a brand book and flags every shot, subtitle, and caption that's out of line before it goes to the client. A legal-compliance agent, meanwhile, checks disclaimers, claim language, music clearance, and on-screen text against rules set by counsel. It's no small check.

Agentic editing, and this world of AI editing agents, may be a lot for some editors to take in all at once. But as seen in Adobe's agent collaboration work across Premiere and elsewhere, like it or not, this is the shape of what's coming.
Eddie AI's Agent Marketplace launches with 29 agents at debut. Plans and pricing are available together on the company's website.
For anyone who wants to talk to the team directly, Eddie AI and co-founder and CEO Shamir Allibhai will be at IBC 2026 in Amsterdam, at Hall 7 booth 7.A38 and the Future Tech Hall booth 14.B51.

Today's befores & afters podcast covered the latest on Autodesk Flow Studio. Readers and listeners of this outlet will remember several past conversations with Nikola Todorovic about AI filmmaking. The company he co-founded, Wonder Dynamics, is now part of Autodesk.

The AI filmmaking tool Nikola and his team built is now called Flow Studio. This news is the launch of 3D Editor + Canvas. Users generate, assemble, render, and refine a scene all inside a single workspace. The idea is to let people grab and shape a scene more directly, a point Nikola made a particular point of in the conversation.
