The podcast also covered the broader currents of machine learning and AI in VFX and CG, and where to be cautious.
Below is a demo video and images showing 3D Editor + Canvas.

Avid Media Composer 2026.8 is out. The biggest change this time is third-party storage support. It's a big enough shift that Avid put out a separate document for it, and it's tied to the $99 upgrade fee for Media Composer Ultimate users moving to Enterprise.

Media Composer now officially supports shared projects on third-party shared storage, including NAS and SAN—but only with a Media Composer Enterprise license. Multiple editors can share bins on the same project and use media on shared storage together. Bin locking shows a green lock when available, a red lock when another editor has it open, and opens read-only in that case.

Edit rooms running Ultimate that have been solving bin-locking with tools like MimicPro now have a choice: stay on their current version and keep doing what they're doing, or move to 2026.8 and take on an Enterprise license. Avid says customers who don't upgrade don't need to do anything.

For anyone cutting interviews or panel talks, the interesting addition is PhraseFind Multicam Auto Cut. You transcribe the multicam clip first, assign a camera angle to each speaker in the transcript tool, load the group clip into a sequence, and hit Auto Cut. Media Composer analyzes the transcript and automatically cuts to whoever is speaking. You refine the result with settings like timing offset and minimum speech length.

blocks.cap: A first line cut built by Auto Cut

blocks.x: The author notes that Avid isn't marketing this as an AI tool. It uses the built-in transcription feature, but the rest is closer to mechanical processing. It can't see a silent person's expression or a good reaction shot, so the idea is to let it handle the first line cut and have an editor go in and refine it.

The transcript tool now has version control. The AI's original transcript stays available, so you can revert the whole thing or just a section at any time. There's also a feature to split a segment in two, an option to merge consecutive segments from the same speaker into one paragraph, and an option to break paragraphs at a default 30-second interval.

blocks.cap: The transcript tool, now with version control

blocks.x: Beyond that, you can now pick the audio track straight from the original master clip when working with subclips and group clips, with gain and volume adjustment included. The column selection window got a search field. In Titler+, keyframes hold up more reliably when you trim, cut, or duplicate clips. The free Media Composer First also grew, with its video/audio track count limits and SD/HD resolution cap removed.

Runway has released GWM Worlds 2. Instead of a model that spits out finished clips, it's a model that runs, in real time, a world you can step into and move around. 720p video at 24fps and 48,000Hz audio stream without interruption.

You first set the environment, characters, visual style, physics, and mood. Once inside, you direct it with text. You can speak to a specific character or to the whole scene—tell someone to swing a sword, have a room fill with water, or bring in a sandstorm. The camera keeps moving independently of all that.

Runway organized this input into a format it calls WorldPrompt, split into two layers: what persists and what changes over time. The front layer holds the Genesis Prompt and first frame, covering scene description, characters, and rules like gravity or collision. The back layer holds actions with start and end timestamps plus frame-level camera input. Actions can overlap, and dialogue counts as one type of action.

A major point is that there's no fixed length. The world doesn't follow a script; it continues from wherever new input arrives. You can walk in first person, then cut to third person, and when characters talk to each other, lip shapes and tone of voice come along with it. You can also feed in existing footage and keep playing from where it leaves off.

Runway sees this model as a foundation for interactive entertainment, virtual characters, and robotics and embodied-agent simulation. Also released alongside it were experiments where an agent was given a character and castle lighting to handle at once, and where it was tasked with navigating between a red flag and a blue flag.

Director Na Hong-jin's Hope combines sci-fi and action. It's set in a fictional port town near Korea's DMZ. After an unidentified alien life-form is discovered, police, hunters, and residents struggle to survive a growing threat. Alicia Vikander and Michael Fassbender play the aliens J'aur and Ma'veyyo, performing them through motion capture.

The film is packed with large-scale action, from police car chases and shootouts to alien creatures tearing through the town and forest. There's even a character who charges in on horseback. Visual effects were key to sculpting the creatures and placing them in scenes, but the crew also held onto the sense that the action was physically grounded—which is why the camera keeps shaking.

Each alien creature looks different from the next. From tentacled forms to ones closer to human shape, most carry the wounds from crash-landing on Earth. Director Na said, 'They all came from different planets, and when they meet in the film, they're bound together as a single front.' That's also why the creature that appears first is left almost formless. Early designs leaned toward realism before the team changed course, moving away from the American creature-design mold toward Asian lines and shapes.

Ma'veyyo, the leader played by Fassbender, normally stands on two legs but shifts into a four-legged beast when chasing humans. It drew a little inspiration from Ridley Scott's Alien, and was designed as a biological transformation rather than a mechanical one. Most scenes featuring the alien creatures were shot with stunt doubles and dummies, with the lead actors' performances added later on a motion capture stage in post-production.

The action was planned in advance through storyboards and previs. The key challenge was keeping the camera close to the actors. Drones, cranes, and cable cams were all used, and XM2 supplied an electric bike fitted with a camera arm, a remote-controlled slider, and a wireless camera vehicle named 'Charlie.' About a dozen horses and vehicles stood ready at a time. Director Na said, 'The lens was only about a foot from the horses' hooves,' adding that it wouldn't have been possible without the stunt team's trust. Because filming happened on location rather than in a controlled studio, practical effects like explosions went off in real time during shooting.

On the motion capture set, the actors wore body suits along with head-mounted cameras (HMC) for their faces. The team used previs to block out movement, and director Na said watching both actors memorize even nonsensical lines word-for-word made him feel their professionalism. Facial performances captured by the HMC were transferred directly onto the digital creatures. Visual effects were led by Westworld, and the hardest part was scale. The gigantic bodies moving at such absurd speed made motion blur stand out, and the team held onto that problem until they got it right.

If you use AI video tools, you'll eventually hit this message: it can't generate the clip because a real person is in it. The same block shows up even on film or ad work done with proper permission. Curious Refuge tested a workaround that's been going around, using it directly on Seedance 2.5.

The method is simple. Before uploading a character reference, you draw a grid over the face to lightly obscure it—just enough to get past the filter while keeping as much identifying information as possible. Both figures got this treatment before moving on to video generation.

There were three tests: a scene with both figures together, a more complex scene with an added location reference, and a cafe scene where the two trade dialogue. Each time, the result was placed side by side with one made from the original, unobscured reference.

It works. But there's a cost. The grid-obscured reference held onto about 80 to 85 percent of the likeness to the original person, and the unobscured reference always produced a more accurate likeness. The loss shows up most in close-ups, dialogue-heavy scenes, or any job where an actor needs to look the same across multiple shots.

If precise character consistency matters, this isn't the first option. But it's a card worth playing when you have permission and the platform keeps rejecting the reference anyway, when the character has distinctive clothing or appearance, or when you just need to get past the block temporarily.

Nuah Studios has opened its AI production platform, Showcraft, to the public. The San Francisco company built the platform to take a starting point—whether that's a script, a shot list, or a single concept image—and carry it through storyboards, animatics, animation, and final editing in one environment. Several AI image and video models run together inside it.

blocks.cap: Noah Wagner's stop-motion-style adult dark comedy “Rainbow Hollow.” Image courtesy of Nuah Studios

blocks.x: What matters is that this isn't a demo. Nuah's first original series—Noah Wagner's stop-motion-style adult dark comedy “Rainbow Hollow”—was made on Showcraft. So was “Astro Burn,” a vertical animated micro-series by HaZ Dulu adapting his own retro pixel-art game.

The user base is growing too. Emmy-winning producer and Bento Box Entertainment co-founder Joel Kuwahara uses it, and writer-director Jerrica Cleland, a former Pixar cinematographer, attached it to her new feature. That feature is being produced by Oscar-nominated animation studio Nøerlum Entertainment, with Nikolaj Coster-Waldau and his production company Ill Kippers as executive producers.

Cleland said, “Combining Showcraft with traditional animation through an artist-led, human-centered approach opens up new creative possibilities while cutting production costs in half. It makes independent films like mine possible.”
On the feature side, it supports ACES color management and HDR/SDR output. The company said local real-time 4K upscaling is in the works.

CEO Silvio Druin explained it this way: “AI can make one shot. The hard problem is turning thousands of shots into a coherent production. Showcraft brings the structure and control of a professional production environment into AI, letting filmmakers focus on story and direction instead of managing a fragmented workflow.”

Pricing is a one-time credit bundle, not a subscription. Generation costs are shown before a render is triggered, and purchased credits stay valid for six months. Subscriptions and add-on tiers launch on October 6, and credits bought during the early access period carry over under those expiration terms.

Runway unveiled Solaris, the first model in a new line the company calls an Interface World Model. The question behind it is simple: what happens if the operating system generates apps and websites while you're using them?

Solaris doesn't turn an interface into code and then run it. It generates the screen itself frame by frame, in real time. When you touch it, the next frame is synthesized to match that action. Because the screen keeps rendering, reflections shift with the lighting and objects respond however they're touched. Unlike software that only accepts prebuilt actions, it can take in completely different behaviors within the same scene.

Here's how it works. Inputs like clicks and drags become the conditioning for the next frame, so the relationship between action and screen is learned rather than programmed separately. Video diffusion models are too slow for interactive use, so Runway went through a three-step process: teaching autoregressive frame generation, distilling denoising down to a few steps, and then retraining on its own outputs. A language model interprets what to do, and Solaris renders how that looks and responds.

The evaluation ran two ways. In the reconstruction fidelity test, multimodal language models like Claude Fable 5, GPT-4o, and Gemini 2.5 Pro were given website screenshots and asked to rebuild the interface, and content preservation was measured using SSIM and DINOv3 features. Performance dropped as screens got more complex, and despite recent years of progress, every language model lost information during reconstruction.

In the user study, 250 people compared Solaris against the latest language model, Claude Opus 5, across 30 interaction scenarios, producing nearly 7,500 pairwise judgments. For following instructions, Solaris scored 61% versus 24% for the code-built interface. For natural-feeling behavior, the gap widened to 71% versus 21%.

The limitations were listed too. Rendering readable text reliably is one of the hardest problems in video generation, yet interfaces depend heavily on text. As an alternative, Runway points to a hybrid approach that splits text-heavy screens off to image models while interaction stays with video models. Factual accuracy is handled by anchoring to a first frame built from real product images and reference material. Maintaining consistency over long interactions and integrating with assistive technology like screen readers are still open problems.
No release date or pricing has been announced. Runway is preparing a full launch with major partners, and early access is being taken through an application form.
The Visual Effects Society (VES) announced new categories and rule changes for the VES Awards. The 25th ceremony will be held on February 17, 2027, at the Beverly Hilton in Los Angeles.

One of the new categories is Outstanding In-Camera Effects in a Photoreal Project. It renames and broadens the existing Outstanding Special (Practical) Effects in a Photoreal Project. It covers results achieved through physical, optical, and mechanical techniques and captured in camera, spanning pyrotechnics, miniatures, and animatronics through special makeup and forced-perspective sets. VES wrote that this expansion honors the fact that work made in the real world remains the foundation of visual effects storytelling.

Another new category is Outstanding Visual Effects in a Short Project. Open to live-action and animation alike for works 45 minutes or under, it accepts short narrative films, short documentaries, music videos, social-media-native content, and experimental films. It also creates a place for artists working outside theatrical and episodic projects.

VES also began splitting animation and live action apart. What was once a single Outstanding CG Cinematography category is now divided into separate live-action and animation categories. The animation category's name changes from Animated Feature to Animated Project, bringing episodic work under its umbrella. The simulation-focused category has been renamed Procedural Effects.

Here's the timeline. Submissions open on September 15, 2026, and close on October 31. The members-only global nomination event is set for January 16, 2027, with finalists announced on January 19. Online viewing and voting run from January 25 through February 7.

If you animate in Maya, you've probably used one of Ehsan Bayat's free tools at some point: Twosify, Pickify, Vectorify, and most recently Animo. He builds them around his own workflow to cut out repetitive work, and he releases every one of them for free. New tools keep coming out too.

This version lets you load references directly inside Maya, accepting every video format along with GIFs and images. Six more animation sliders were added as well. The biggest change is the new tool editor: it surfaces more than 500 tools on a single screen, lets you assign hotkeys or pin them straight to the shelf, and even lets you register your own animation tools.
On top of that come bug fixes and performance improvements, plus a pass at cleaning up the UI flow.

Here's what's packed into Animo: selection sets, pose and animation mirroring, animation sliders, a graph editor toolbar, a fast arc tracker and a camera-space arc tracker, left-right key nudging, temporary pivots, space switching and attribute space switching, global offset, Xform, a Spider-Verse style animation tool, animation repathing, copying animation and poses between scenes, quick object export and import, fast baking, translate/rotate/scale reset, an animation layer tool, and a multi-camera playblaster.
Animo is still in beta, with a notice that bugs may remain, and it's available to download from the release page. A few days ago, he also introduced STUDIOJOIN's free full-body Maya rig.

Liu Haonan and Cao Yihang have been stitching together each other's stories since high school. Ten years on, the two of them build a 30-light-year-scale sci-fi universe almost entirely by themselves, using AI production tools instead of a camera crew.

blocks.cap: Key visual for the TapNow AI screening at the Venice Production Bridge

blocks.x: Scale used to require budget, people, and infrastructure, which is largely why the authority to tell big stories sat with Hollywood. AI production tools have begun to shake up that arrangement, and this year the companies building those tools gathered in Venice.

At the center of it is Palo Alto-based Tamar AI. The company says it's building creative infrastructure for the AI era by combining production tools, a streaming platform, and IP incubation. Its flagship product, TapNow, is an AI-native creative operating system that packs multimodal AI, agents, and production workflows into a single environment. According to the company, it's used by more than 3 million people a day across 150 countries and regions.

Tian Shu, head of global AI product solutions at technology partner Alibaba Token Hub, put it this way: “AI doesn't replace the people who make films. It just narrows the distance between what you imagine and what you can see.”

Sitting on top of that is 10,000 Parallel Universes, a creator and IP incubation program. The first season drew more than 2,000 submissions, with prize money topping $500,000. Selected teams received computing resources, and in some cases production funding as well. The company says it didn't take copyright in return.

Liu and Cao's「Primordia」is the program's flagship title. It's set among a cluster of star systems the pair call Ore, where a war breaks out over resources mined from ancient creatures. Cao sees the appeal of AI filmmaking less in the tools than in the scale. “In the past, even one location shoot for a short film needed 30 to 40 people. They'd all come ask what's next, and the creative flow kept getting interrupted.” Liu's reason is simpler. “In the end, it came down to people. In traditional production, you sometimes spend more time on people and admin than on the work itself.”

HappyHorse handles the infrastructure side. It's a video generation model inside Alibaba Token Hub (ATH), the independent business group Alibaba Group set up in March. Rather than a finishing tool, it's built to let people preview and test ideas early, during the planning stage, and it covers everything from concept exploration to previsualization. It served as technology partner on three of the program's entries, and all three are heading to Venice as award winners.

The two companies are co-hosting programming at the Venice Production Bridge. The panel AI + Cinema: The Next Generation of Storytelling and Creativity runs on September 4 at the Hotel Excelsior, followed by the selections screening New Voices in AI Cinema on September 7 at the Palazzo del Casino.

Where TapNow is heading is Glanze. Every title starts as a preview called a Glance before growing into episodes and seasons. The web version launched on September 4 with more than 40 series Glances posted, five of which are moving into full serialization. The mobile app arrives in late October, carrying more than 30 serialized shows and more than 100 Glances to browse.
Corridor Crew spends 56 seconds on just one thing: rotoscoping. The question is what separates good roto from bad roto.

Answering it is VFX supervisor Marion Spates. She's been Emmy-nominated and has worked on Stranger Things, WandaVision, Lost in Space, and the recent Avatar: The Last Airbender. In the video, she shares one tip that could change how you think about it.
There's also the story of her first VFX job: rotoscoping Matthew McConaughey in Reign of Fire.
Curious Refuge unveiled an AI workflow in a new video that extracts new camera coverage using only existing footage. The video is titled 「This AI Workflow Is Flipping Filmmaking Upside Down.」
Using this technique, it is possible to newly create angles from existing footage that were never actually captured on set.
The workflow was devised by Christopher Gwinn, and the channel said it also posted a detailed write-up of the process on its blog.
It was introduced as a technique that could give editors and directors a new option in situations where reshoots are difficult or coverage is lacking.

This episode of the fxpodcast meets Crafty Apes CEO Alana Newell to hear about her journey from hands-on compositing artist to studio executive, and how her yardstick for success has changed in that seat.

As an artist, Newell found satisfaction in finishing a shot and seeing the completed frame. But now, leading a company of about 400 people across eight offices, visible moments of victory are far rarer.

"For me, every win ultimately belongs to our team," she says. "It's a success we achieved together." Conversely, when a mistake happens, she added that the personal weight she feels is different, "since this seat is responsible for the whole company's results."

The experience she built on production floors still carries directly into Newell's leadership today. How she prices project bids, gauges risk, and communicates with artists all comes from that experience. It is also part of why Crafty Apes has earned a reputation as a nimble, resourceful company that moves freely between big tentpole films and smaller projects that need a careful hand.

Taking on work of different scales at the same time is also a kind of management strategy. Rather than relying on a handful of big titles, Crafty Apes spreads its exposure widely. Newell says a studio spread across 50 projects can absorb schedule changes far more safely than a studio dependent on five major clients.

Technology is also part of this strategy, though Newell's focus doesn't stop at the generative AI that's getting all the attention these days. VFX companies have already accumulated years of production data covering schedules, shot difficulty, and actual delivery timing. Her view is that machine learning can use this data to sharpen the accuracy of bidding, staffing, and project selection.
"For machine learning, the VFX pipeline isn't a 'bug,' it's a 'feature,'" she says.

Crafty Apes also encourages its artists to build broader skill sets. Newell believes the newly emerging tools in the industry favor people who are curious and adaptable over applicants who lean on years of experience in one specific area. Growing talent in-house matters too, but she considers outside talent and ideas the key source of creative stimulation.

The 「The Wizard of Oz」 work done at Sphere was a case of applying traditional VFX know-how to an entirely new format. Newell said she also sees opportunities in immersive entertainment, interactive installations, museums, and theme park attractions, and that there is in fact an ongoing project with Universal.

To her, this isn't simply about adding one more adjacent market. It's closer to expanding the very definition of what Crafty Apes can become. "I think of Crafty not as a VFX company but as a content production company," Newell says. "If you need footage, we'll make it for you."
Director Danny Boyle has admitted to using AI in his new film 「Ink,」 which depicts the founding of The Sun.

In an interview with Vanity Fair, Boyle said he used generative AI for about 30 seconds of footage in the new film, which opened the Venice International Film Festival. The film was subsequently invited to the Telluride Film Festival as well.

"There's about 30 seconds in the film where two old photographs are animated into motion," he said in a video interview conducted in Telluride, Colorado. "Oh, and there are also rats. AI is particularly strong at rendering animals, and that's how we made the rats running through The Sun's newsroom," he added.

Some viewers posted on social media wondering whether old photos of the Kray brothers and former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher had been revived with AI in the film, and footage from the Telluride event suggests that was indeed the case.

When Vanity Fair earlier asked how he felt about the film's use of AI, Boyle answered as follows: "What does my opinion matter? What matters is what 20-year-olds think. That's the honest answer. For me, AI is a useful tool in many ways. But that comes with the condition that it's used in a respectful way, and if an actor is replaced with AI, that actor has to be fairly compensated."
Even before that, Boyle had voiced concerns about AI's impact on journalism and other industries at the 「Ink」 press conference held in Venice.

"Big Tech and their AI are dangerous because they could replace journalism itself. They will build more efficient and cheaper AI journalists, but will an AI journalist built that way be able to speak truth to the power that created it?"

「Ink」 stars Jack O'Connell, Guy Pearce, and Claire Foy, and depicts the rise of Britain's notorious tabloid The Sun in the 1970s, under editor Larry Lamb, who was recruited from the Daily Mirror by Rupert Murdoch.

Produced by StudioCanal and Netflix, the film is set for a theatrical release in December and a Netflix release in January, and has been largely well received in Venice, currently holding an 85% score on Rotten Tomatoes.
If you are looking for an easy way to add footsteps to your project, the Krotos workflow now built into Premiere and Resolve is worth a look.
Recording footsteps and other foley yourself takes time and budget most editors do not have, so many fill in sound effects with royalty-free audio or whatever source is on hand.

Editors looking to add elements like footsteps have more options these days. The Footsteps workflow in the Krotos Studio plugin is one of them, running directly inside major NLEs such as Adobe Premiere and DaVinci Resolve.
Here is what to know.
The feature extends Krotos Video to Sound. Through the Krotos Studio plugin, the Footsteps workflow now works inside Adobe Premiere and DaVinci Resolve.
Footsteps reads the motion in a video clip to identify where feet land, then builds a sound pass synced to the edit.
You review the result right inside the Krotos Studio plugin. Swapping the suggested floor material or shoe, adjusting levels, and nudging individual footsteps forward or back all happen there.

For editors and sound designers adding footsteps and adjusting timing, it is one of the quicker, easier options. You do not have to leave the timeline even for the fiddly parts, like floor changes or uneven footstep pace.
On pricing and terms, the feature is included with Krotos Video to Sound. Plans and pricing are listed on the Krotos website.
Blender Studio has opened the doors on OVERGROWN, its animated project in the works. Behind-the-scenes articles and educational material are free for anyone to view for a while.

During the limited-run Open Doors Week, Blender artists can look at how the upcoming teaser was assembled over several months. Six production logs cover everything from early development through animation, shading, lighting, effects, music and final compositing.
The material covers character rigs and fur setups, voice casting, set construction, hand-tuned shading detail, shot animation and final visual development.
One entry focuses on how water was handled, including lighting and dripping-water effects. The last entry covers score composition and the finished composite.
Simon Thommes' Painterly Shadows masterclass was released alongside it, covering the stylized shadow technique behind OVERGROWN's distinct illustrated look.
Even while preparing the teaser release, Blender Studio describes OVERGROWN not as another finished Blender open movie but as a project that could become a feature film.
The current stage has gone toward refining the concept, testing the visual direction, and leaving behind knowledge the Blender community can keep using.

Open Doors Week also doubles as an effort to bring in more subscribers. The studio says it has not yet reached its goal of 7,000 subscribers, and that number is what it says it needs to carry OVERGROWN into the next stage.
Subscription fees support Blender Studio's films and educational material, downloadable assets, and work that feeds back into developing Blender itself.
The full material is available on the OVERGROWN project page.
befores & afters featured a Wētā FX VFX breakdown video for season 3 of “House of the Dragon.” The line attached to it: there is ship-to-ship combat, and no shortage of dragons.
In the video description, Wētā FX names the work as the Battle of the Gullet from season 3.
For this sequence, the studio built a massive environment stretching from Driftmark to Dragonstone.
A ship actually built on set was extended into a smoke-filled battlefield.
The dragon Sheepstealer also makes its first appearance here.
The reference painting was Turner's “The Battle of Trafalgar.” Scale, spectacle and a turning point in the story all come together in a single opening, the studio says.

Wētā FX is a studio headquartered in Wellington, New Zealand, with creative hubs in Vancouver, Canada and Melbourne, Australia. Combining artists, engineers and management, it has more than 2,000 people.
An in-house pipeline built by the studio itself runs the show, supplying artists with tools and infrastructure.

Over more than 30 years, its awards include 8 Academy Awards for visual effects, 17 Academy Scientific and Technical Awards, 8 BAFTA awards for visual effects, and 61 VES Awards from its peers. It is also the studio behind Gollum, Kong, Neytiri, Caesar, Pogo, and the Middle-earth and Pandora they live in.

blocks.cap: Art of the Frame Podcast: The Alan Smithee Round Table

blocks.x: The Alan Smithee Round Table opened its fifth season. It is hosted by Scott Simmons, Katie Hinsen and Michael Kammes. The episode first pays tribute to several industry figures who have passed, then moves straight into news shaking up Hollywood.
Starting with the industry numbers, the 2026 box office is running 15% above last year. With Paramount, Fox and Disney all making moves, business models are shifting at every level.
On the technology side, the software landscape is splitting fast. New currents in AI and immersive media have taken hold, and post-production tools appear to be racing to keep pace.

Adobe's acquisition of Topaz Labs brought AI upscaling directly into its own tools. On the other side, Avid has begun requiring the pricier Media Composer Enterprise for project sharing, and into that gap Hedge has acquired Mimic to offer an alternative for smaller post houses.

The conversation then turns to each host's own work: how Kammes has been integrating AI into his workflow, Hinsen's visit to the AlloSphere at UCSB, and the EditSwitch project Simmons has been devoted to.
Runway posted a four-minute-15-second short called “Full Metal Lunchbox” on its official channel. The only description given is a single line: a story about chasing down a broccoli who went AWOL.

Rather than a short demo, it's broken into chapters like a feature film. It opens with “Breaking the Beach Bridgehead,” followed by “The Last Devotion of the Pea,” “Welcome to the Salad,” and “Clam Shell Shock.”
The back half closes with “Death of a Salad Salesman,” “Melting Point” and “All Quiet on the Dinner Front.” It's a structure that moves the conventions of war movies onto the dinner table.

What's worth watching is not the subject matter but the length. Whether a single cut can hold character and tone for more than four minutes shows just how far today's generative video tools can be pushed.
The Ulanzi AU05 VibeKey is a hard thing to categorize. According to the manufacturer, it's a compact AI workflow controller aimed at photo and video creators.
Ulanzi recommends using it alongside major voice-input software. It supports AI agents such as ChatGPT, Claude and Codex, as well as voice-input tools like Typeless.

It consists of three customizable keys, a smart control knob and a built-in microphone. The idea is to speak to AI and press frequently used shortcuts to speed up everything from shoot planning to captions and editing notes.
The microphone picks up commands while the voice key is held down. You can throw out a prompt without moving your hands far, even while coding, writing or editing.
Key assignments can be reconfigured in Ulanzi Studio, keeping your most-used commands right at your fingertips.
The battery is 300mAh, 3.7V, 1.1Wh. It charges in about four hours over USB-C and is said to last up to five days under a work mode of three continuous hours of use per day.
It's priced at $61.59 and is available now.

Ahead of IBC 2026, Adobe released updates to Premiere Pro and After Effects. There's a lot of AI in them, but some of it is actually useful, Scott Simmons opened by saying. The lineup mixes shipped features and betas, from a tool that generates footage inside the timeline to an AI assistant for After Effects that writes expressions for you.

blocks.cap: Draw a range on a track, write a prompt, and a clip is generated right there

blocks.x: The generative media tool becomes a full feature in Premiere this week at IBC. Draw a range anywhere on a track, describe what you need, and it's generated without leaving the app. The tool sits where the generative extension used to live on the toolbar, and a long press switches between the two. You pick a reference frame from the timeline or the program monitor with an eyedropper, write a prompt, and choose a model. Premiere matches the sequence settings, so the clip comes out at the edit's resolution and aspect ratio. The credit cost shows up in the taskbar before you run it.

You can pick a model from Adobe Firefly, Google Veo, Kling, Runway or Luma. The same tool also generates sound effects on audio tracks. You draw a range and write a prompt, but you can also record your own voice to set the timing and intensity. Results come back as four variations, and all of them are saved to the project.

blocks.cap: Generate Soundscape skips the prompt and reads only the footage to pull four tracks

blocks.x: Two more features arrived in beta. Generate Music uses the Firefly Music model to take a prompt and a target BPM and produce royalty-free background music, letting you choose between an intro/outro structure or a seamless loop. Generate Soundscape skips the prompt entirely. It reads the footage above the selected range and pulls four pre-mixed tracks — two ambience, two effects — matched to the action. Simmons wrote that the results were uneven: some tracks were usable, others were out of sync.

blocks.cap: Enhance Audio splits a mixed clip into dialogue, music, ambience and effects

blocks.x: The new AI audio tools in the Premiere beta target bad sound that's already in your project. Enhance Audio splits a mixed clip into dialogue, music, ambience and effects, each with its own slider. Separate Sound Sources exports those channels to their own physical tracks. Separate Crosstalk splits audio where two speakers were recorded over each other into two tracks, with the remainder going to a third track. Dynamic Auto Ducking generates ducking keyframes automatically, and regenerates them whenever you move a clip.

blocks.cap: Color mode gets new HSL and luminance masks

blocks.x: Color mode is still in beta, but features have been landing fast since its NAB debut. Auto Color is a starting point that sets white balance and exposure in one pass, and it runs the same way whether you apply it to a single clip, a selected group, or an entire sequence. HSL masks and luminance masks isolate specific ranges of hue, saturation or brightness and attach them to clip adjustments. A vignette module and a midtones module also arrived in beta.

After Effects gets an AI assistant in public beta. It operates across the whole project rather than just the open comp. Describe the motion you want, and it writes an expression rig with sliders using JavaScript, then breaks down what it built in a table. If an expression breaks, you can just ask it to fix it. It can also scan an inherited project with hundreds of layers, propose an organizational structure, and execute it once you approve. Every action can be undone.

In a press demo, Jason Druss used a Photoshop file to build a '90s-style stop-motion collage animation. With a single prompt, he rigged expressions across six photo-frame precomps and added sliders for wiggle amount, frame rate and stack spacing.

'Astro Burn,' the bullet-hell shooter from independent game studio Beyond the Pixels, has taken its next step as an animated micro-series. Episode 1 is available on TikTok, YouTube Shorts and Instagram. In the game, players become the space cat Astro, fighting through absurd obstacles and enemies alongside a robot companion to get home.

Haz Dulull, the London-based developer, director and producer who made the game, teamed up with Nura Studio to turn 'Astro Burn' into ten one-minute vertical episodes. They were made with Nura's Showcraft platform, based in Montreal and Los Angeles, which reworked the game's characters and world for social media scrolling.

Here's how Dulull put it: “Showcraft was designed for producers and creators like me who care deeply about their own IP. I wanted full control over a locked model trained only on my own assets, so that 'Astro Burn's' visual identity would stay intact all the way through.”

Abe Schuermann, a writer and director at Nura Studio who worked closely with Dulull as showrunner and producer, developed and finished each episode in roughly one working week. That covers the script, animation, sound design, voice recording, music, cleanup and final delivery.

Even the first test frames were trained only on the original character sprites, animation and artwork that Dulull provided. “When I sent notes, revisions came back in hours, sometimes faster, with the feedback reflected exactly. That kind of turnaround is rare for a showrunner.”

The team stresses that people led the production from start to finish. Graziella LaRocca voices Astro, Elvis Deane voices AL, and Brian Wolwich plays several supporting roles in rotation. The music was written by human composers and licensed through Epidemic Sound, then edited to picture. Schuermann puts it this way: “A human voice actor brings nuance that's mostly absent in AI voices. We feel the same about the music.”

Showcraft didn't replace a traditional creative team — it let a small group, made up of one IP owner and showrunner, one writer-director, three voice actors and a licensed composer, finish a project that would normally have needed months and far more resources. Dulull, who was initially skeptical of generative AI, sums it up this way: “AI doesn't tell your story for you. That's still your job. This works because the technology supports a clear creative vision, not because you can feed it any idea and pull out any shot.”

Nura sees this adaptation as a practical model for indie game developers to expand their IP and reach new audiences. Isabelle Riva, Nura Studio's executive producer and VP of content, said “micro-series are a powerful way to get indie developers' games discovered where players are already spending their time.” The ten episodes release one per day over ten days.

Blackmagic Design released DaVinci Resolve 21.1. It brings AI assistant integration, the hottest topic in editing software right now, along with more than 100 new tools and controls. Photo support and camera formats also expanded, and a long list of changes landed for editing speed and color grading.

It reads like two announcements folded into one. The first is yet another major update. Blackmagic hasn't let up on its push to make Resolve the primary choice for editors and colorists. Its push into multimedia editing continues as well, with the photo editing side gaining expanded support and new camera formats.
The other announcement is AI assistant integration, an area that until now has mostly belonged to third-party apps and tools like Edey AI or Nice Touch.

On the Media page, you can now edit text and checkboxes in list view, and search scans down into sub-bins with exact text matching. There's also a feature to change the start timecode of multiple clips at once. The Cut and Edit pages gained Inspector presets, a new comparison timeline workflow, and shortcut switching across up to 25 multicam angles. The trim editor refines with mouse drag and nudge.

The Color page now reads DJI D-Gamut2 and D-Log2, GoPro Log, Leica L-Log, and Vivo's wide gamut and Vivo Log. Fusion gained Crocodove-based shape and 3D tools along with OpenPBR material shader support. In general items, it natively supports NVIDIA RTX Spark systems on Windows, and HEIC decoding gets hardware acceleration on Apple silicon. HTJ2K-compressed EXR rendering is now possible too.

At the end of the release notes is a line editing suites will chew on. Python scripting has moved to the Studio edition. Blackmagic's explanation is that the Python API was being used to bolt Studio features onto the free version. The company added that it covers its engineering team's costs through Studio license sales, taking a different path from subscriptions that charge monthly and lock your work if you don't pay.

blocks.cap: 'Thunderbolts,' worked on by Rising Sun Pictures

blocks.x: Today's episode of the Before and Afters podcast featured Troy Tobin of Pitch Black. He currently serves as head of research and innovation for REVIZE.

REVIZE is a proprietary machine learning technology that came out of Rising Sun Pictures. Studio artists have used it on films like 'Sinners,' 'Mickey 17,' 'Thunderbolts,' 'Furiosa' and 'Thor: Love and Thunder.'
The core of this announcement is expansion. REVIZE is moving beyond Rising Sun to other studios under Pitch Black — namely FOLKS, El Ranchito and Square One.
On the podcast, Tobin and Ian Failes discuss that expansion. They also cover how REVIZE was built, where it's been used, and where it's headed next.

Before and Afters has covered REVIZE multiple times before, including how Rising Sun Pictures' machine learning technology was built, the face swaps and lasers in the most chaotic scene of 'Sonic the Hedgehog 3,' tweening technology, and how young Furiosa was made.
Is a Hollywood story editor especially vulnerable to AI? What about a concept illustrator, or a sound mixer?

An ongoing project the Creators Coalition on AI (CCAI) is launching on Wednesday takes on exactly those questions. Officially called the Standards & Definitions Project, it opens with a website aimed at the industry. CCAI is a group formed nine months ago by around a dozen people, including Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Daniel Kwan, and late-night program veteran Ted Trempe. It favors keeping creation in the AI era human-led.

blocks.cap: Hiro Murai and Daniel Kwan at a keynote conversation at the 2024 Film Independent Forum.

blocks.x: The web portal starts with a glossary of roughly 180 AI-related terms, meant to put previously shifting language on common ground.

An “AI Impact Visualizer” also goes live alongside it. It rates roughly 150 jobs across 11 creative areas — direction, sound, animation, screenwriting, acting, and more — on a scale from 0 (“doesn't touch that work”) to 5 (“can do the whole job”). Many of those jobs are further broken down into dozens of sub-items.
More than 250 people have responded so far, but the goal is thousands. Most jobs are still marked as “recommended knowledge,” a sign that not enough data has been gathered yet.

“The point of this material is to gather all the stories floating around about AI and build a factual floor,” Trempe said in an interview. “It's not the destination of what we're trying to do. It just sets up a process people can keep pace with.”

He admits the survey can't capture every case: a hairdresser who scored a 0 is still affected once a set goes virtual. Still, the founders see this as having started to translate what was once vague back-and-forth into numbers. “I hope people end up with a tool to speak more clearly instead of vague fear,” said Trempe, who produced “The AI Doc” this year.

The Impact Visualizer and glossary arrive on Wednesday after two “conventions” last summer that brought together guild representatives from all 11 areas. Human-authored content, for instance, is defined as “work to which a generative AI system has not contributed expressive content,” and using a camera, instrument, editing software, or an AI system that performs purely technical functions doesn't count against that.

The definitions were hashed out through back-and-forth at the conventions and aren't set in stone, Trempe says; they'll change based on member input. CCAI's signatories number in the thousands, including Judd Apatow, Ava DuVernay, Margot Robbie, and Guillermo del Toro.

The founders hope the shared language will be used everywhere from guild negotiations to individual contracts. CCAI founder and the group's convener, writer-director David Goyer, said “CCAI's Standards & Definitions Project is about turning confusion into clarity, and clarity into the capacity to act.” Trempe also cited an easier path to drafting and passing state legislation as a use case.

CCAI will keep refining the terms and impact assessments, with major updates each quarter. People can add their own experience to the survey page, which verifies whether they work in Hollywood. In a statement timed to the launch, Gordon-Levitt said, “To me, this is bigger than Hollywood. Artists and creators are the canary in the coal mine.” Kwan added his own line: “If we're going to fight for transparency, we have to show it ourselves first.”

The vertical drama industry in its current form began in China. The duanju format spread explosively through the pandemic. When reports emerged that AI-made vertical dramas were flooding the Chinese market and production workers were worried about their jobs, it was an ominous sign for the nascent U.S. market too.

blocks.cap: Against a backdrop of circuit boards, a robotic hand holds up two vertical drama leads.

blocks.x: Companies targeting the U.S. market are also testing whether these short AI stories work. There are apps like My Muse and Inkitt Ironblood that release only AI vertical dramas, and major players like DramaBox, DramaWave, and FlareFlow are also expanding synthetic actors and backgrounds, filling their apps with prompt-generated video.

For workers around LA, that shift is directly a question of work. After traditional jobs vanished following the 2023 Hollywood strikes, vertical dramas served as a livelihood for actors and crew. Now, vertical drama workers in LA tell The Hollywood Reporter that work that was once reliable has noticeably dried up.

“People who worked full-time in this business for years are going back to old jobs, back home. Actors, crew, producers alike,” said Candace Mizga, co-founder of Chera TV, a vertical drama platform that doesn't use AI, and an actor herself. “These last couple of months especially have been huge.”

The cost gap is clear. While live-action vertical drama budgets generally run $100,000 to $300,000, a convincing feature-length AI vertical drama can be made for $60,000 to $100,000, according to AI vertical drama studio Axis AI Studios. Timelines differ too: 12 weeks for live-action versus 2 weeks for AI, figures cited by Holywater Tech, which owns the all-AI app My Muse.

Where a live-action shoot once required 50 people over seven days, “now five people can make an episode in seven days,” said Guy Shimoni, CEO and co-founder of Shortical, a platform that releases both live-action and AI content. He explained that the video generator Seedance 2.0, released in February, accelerated adoption. “Once Seedance 2.0 came out, everyone started using it.”

Auditions are drying up. Maddie Grove, a manager at LEWK Management, said that “by June, casting notices that once posted 15 to 20 a day had dropped to around four.” Actor Kylie Carson says vertical drama auditions that numbered 5 to 15 a week last year are down to two now.

blocks.cap: On an LA set, a makeup artist preps Carter Harvey, lead of CandyJar's vertical drama “Fight Dirty,” for a close-up.

blocks.x: Consent has become an issue too. Actors told Business Insider in July that their performances and likenesses from live-action vertical dramas were used in all-AI projects without permission. Grove says she's seen four cases since June of platforms violating the AI clauses in actors' contracts.

Writers aren't spared either. Tess Dinerstein sold a pirate-themed vertical drama script to DramaBox in 2025, and around the time she finished revisions in 2026, she told an executive she hoped it wouldn't be made with AI. Months later, that executive left the company, and the project came out as an AI production.

In China, more than 95 percent of new vertical dramas in the first quarter of 2026 were reportedly made with AI. Whether AI vertical dramas end up as a passing spectacle in the U.S. is ultimately up to viewers. Martina Monti, an actor who has shot 40 vertical dramas, puts it this way: “Some people are more optimistic about the future — they just hope this AI bubble pops. Others, I don't know.” Right now, she added, it just isn't working well.
Studio Network Solutions (SNS), which makes shared storage hardware and software, unveiled workflow updates at this year's IBC. They focus on performance, compatibility, convenience and flexibility.

blocks.cap: The SNS AI Suite interface running on a laptop.

blocks.x: The company said the latest EVO OS update boosts total throughput by up to 40% on some SSD-equipped EVO 8 Bay and 16 Bay systems. OS-level tuning and system memory optimization raise read and write performance while using less processing power.

The freed-up capacity goes to background automation and 4K projects with multiple editors working at once. It already ships on new EVO systems, and eligible systems running EVO OS 7.1.0 get it for free.

SNS also introduced AI Suite Advanced, a higher tier for on-premises media analysis. It adds natural-language chat and agent features, and its interface has been refined to match the rest of the SNS ecosystem.

The existing AI Suite offers media analysis features such as transcription, translation, summarization and semantic search using multiple AI models. In Advanced, asking questions about material in the media library brings contextual answers. Users can describe tasks in plain language, such as asking it to find clips matching certain conditions or build an EDL from those clips.
AI Suite and Advanced are sold outright as a perpetual license with no limit on AI processing time. Processing happens within the facility, so a company's media never leaves its own walls.

Outpost has started accepting browser uploads. Participants such as producers, assistant editors and clients can upload media files from a compatible browser, including mobile, to run review and approval. Both existing and new Outpost users can use it without first logging into ShareBrowser MAM or Adobe Premiere.

EVO has been validated for use with Avid Media Composer 2026.8 Enterprise, including shared projects and bin locking. SNS was among the vendors selected for beta testing ahead of the public release, and both SNS and Avid confirmed the workflow runs as intended.

blocks.cap: The EVO OS update raises total throughput by up to 40% on some systems.

blocks.x: SNS also plans to release Media Composer training materials through Avid Learning Central and the SNS Training Academy. For facilities that need to upgrade their Avid license to use shared projects and bin locking in Media Composer 2026.8, SNS is offering a discount on new EVO systems to offset that cost.

Transcode Accelerator, EVO's engine for coordinating proxy generation, now extends to Windows workstations in addition to Mac. It pools resources across multiple EVO servers and Mac and Windows workstations running Adobe Media Encoder. Instead of waiting for one machine to finish its queue in sequence, it spreads the proxy and transcoding load across multiple pieces of hardware.

ShareBrowser Admin, which creates and manages custom metadata templates, now also comes as an EVO plugin. It opens right where administrators already open EVO, and even lets them adjust the field order within a template. A podcast library might use season, episode and date as fields; a college athletics department might use semester, sport, opponent, content type and venue status. The tighter the structure, the faster and more accurate the search.
Acon Digital has released Acoustica 8, the new version of its audio editing, restoration, and mastering suite.

This release answers directly the technical problems working engineers have raised. It packs in a set of assistive AI and machine-learning tools that speed up work without cutting into sound quality. Acon says Acoustica 8 was designed not to replace experienced audio professionals but to empower them. Complex restoration tasks, from dialogue cleanup to spectral recovery, are handed to machine learning, while engineers keep full control.

Unlike the broader shift toward subscription software, Acon Digital continues to offer perpetual licenses for its editing, restoration, and mastering tools, leaving buyers the option to purchase without a subscription.

Among the features, DeNoise 3 and DeHum 3 now run on machine-learning models, so there is no need to capture a noise profile first. DeClip 3 and DeClick 3 have a redesigned interface. Extract:Dialogue 2 adds sliders and sensitivity controls for voice, noise, and reverb respectively. Audiophile fills much wider stretches of time with generated content, making recovery smoother.

The spectral editor gains a “Similar Selection” tool that finds regions with properties close to the current selection, along with time and frequency feathering that refines the blend at edit boundaries. A stereo view plots stereo position as color on the spectrogram, letting engineers see balance problems instead of just hearing them.

Immersive audio support, including Dolby Atmos, reaches up to 9.1.6 channels in the Ultimate edition. The UI has been redesigned throughout, adding a new startup screen, a dockable processing tool window, and a customizable toolbar. ARA2 integration comes to every edition, giving access to the full clip editor inside any ARA2 host, while a dedicated link plugin handles AAX transfer with Avid Pro Tools. The lineup has three editions — Standard, Premium, and Ultimate — all sold under perpetual licenses.

Maxon is previewing its fall Maxon One release exclusively at its booth at IBC2026, running September 11 through 14 at the RAI Amsterdam, Hall 7, booth 7.B24. The preview also rounds up the updates made to Cinema 4D, ZBrush, Redshift, Red Giant, and Autograph over the past year. The October release plans will not be officially announced for a few more weeks.

“We keep listening to artists and building the technology underneath our products, so every release opens up more creative possibilities,” said Maxon CEO David McGavran. “A lot happens between the big releases. We're building a technology stack that keeps supporting creativity, so artists can do today what they couldn't do a year ago. IBC is a chance to see what we've built, experience the latest updates, and get an exclusive first look at the booth at what's coming next.”

By product, Cinema 4D moves into a next generation with features for building, populating, and simulating complex 3D worlds. ZBrush tightens the sculpting workflow that links desktop and iPad, cutting down on switching between apps. Redshift gets major performance and interactivity improvements, along with procedural fur and a more cinematic color workflow. AI relighting belongs to Red Giant: a tool called Scene Light speeds up complex lighting changes while leaving control with the artist. Autograph continues its performance and stability work and ties in more deeply with Maxon's tools.

The recap also covers what's already shipped this year. Cinema 4D gained a new UV editor with professional unwrapping and packing, seam editing, texel density tools, and UDIM support, plus Edge, Rivet, and UV Projection modes for Cloner distribution and a fabric brush that lets artists shape soft materials directly in the viewport using the simulation system. ZBrush received native Windows on Arm support, direct Substance Painter integration, and ZModeler improvements. Redshift became more responsive when adjusting lighting and materials, with a new memory architecture and cleaned-up material workflows inside Cinema 4D following along. Red Giant modernized core Universe effects such as Glow, Chromatic Aberration, and RGB Separation with a focus on performance, and brought Cinema 4D's procedural noise into Universe as Maxon Noise.

Autograph, the free motion graphics and compositing app relaunched this year and opened up for commercial use starting in May, now uses Red Giant effects natively and fully supports OpenFX for third-party plugins. It also gained vertical text and CJK typography along with a USD-based 3D workspace, bringing extruded text, shapes, textures, and multi-pass compositing into a single environment.

Booth presentations will feature production teams from WWE, RTL, Imaginary Forces, Fall Off the Wall, and the BBC, along with demos from Maxon trainers Jonas Pilz, Elli Wade, and Chad Perkins. Maxon and Lenovo are hosting a community meetup at Aloha Amsterdam after the show floor closes on Saturday, September 12.
Nice Touch has released Nice Touch V2, the new version of its AI editing assistant for professional post-production teams.
More than 300 conversations with editors, producers, production supervisors, and studio heads set the direction. V2 runs inside Adobe Premiere Pro and DaVinci Resolve, rebuilt from scratch.

Nice Touch is a UK company founded in 2025. Circus Street founders Rich Townsend and Jonny Townsend put in pre-seed funding and both sit on the board. It lets editors hand off the mechanical front-end work without leaving the tools they already use.
Built by two editors with 12 years in the industry, V2 takes on front-end labor like selects, stringouts, assembly, multicam passes, and cutdowns. It supports 18 languages.

It analyzes a project's footage to transcribe it with word-level accuracy and speaker separation, then takes instructions in plain language. When an editor says the cut they want, it builds it straight onto the timeline with real clips, cuts, and markers. From there, the editor just keeps working.

Two things kept coming up across the 300-plus conversations: existing AI tools made editors step outside the edit to process elsewhere and bring the results back in, and editors have lines they don't want to hand over. What turned around a 30-year editor who had avoided AI tools entirely was that Nice Touch “doesn't touch creative judgment.”

Founders Matthew Cooksey and Paul Simon spent 12 years growing Circus Street's video production organization to 200 people, making TV- and VFX-grade content for Coca-Cola, Nike, Nestlé, and Pfizer. Cooksey built a £500,000 virtual studio that sent 60 hours of content in 20 languages to more than 500,000 viewers. Circus Street was sold to QA for £50 million.
“For 12 years, whenever we hit something the tools couldn't do, we built it ourselves. This is the same instinct, just with better technology behind it now,” said Paul Simon, CPO and co-founder.

V2 is available now at nicetouch.app. A five-day free trial comes with 2,000 credits unlocking every feature; paid tiers are Pro at £50 a month for 7,000 credits and Ultra at £250 a month for 40,000 credits. Extra credits can be purchased as needed. Pricing is set in pounds, dollars, and euros. Podimo and the University of Georgia's School of Social Work editing team are already using it.
Amazon Prime Video is making English dubbing look more natural. It uses AI to match the way actors' mouths move on screen.

The first title to get it is the German romance “Maxton Hall,” Prime Video's most-watched international original series to date. The lip-sync dubbing rolls out worldwide in English starting Wednesday for seasons 1 and 2, and it will also be in the final season 3, premiering December 9. Season 3 is based on the 2018 novel “Save Me” by Mona Kasten.
The Prime Video team built the feature by combining AI and VFX technology, though it did not say which AI tools it used. Amazon said it plans to expand the feature to other titles going forward.
The feature matches an actor's lip movements to a human-recorded dub performance. Amazon described the result as “a seamless viewing experience that keeps audiences fully immersed in the story.”

“Prime Video is constantly building new tools that elevate the viewing experience for customers,” said Raf Soltanovich, Vice President of Technology at Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios. “Lip-sync paves the way for customers to enjoy content from around the world more seamlessly and immersively. For creators, it makes it easier for their stories to reach a wider global audience. It's all done under the creator's direction, preserving the integrity of their artistic intent.”
Amazon added that Prime Video will keep looking for practical, useful applications of AI “with the customer at the center and creators in the driver's seat.”
Beeble has unveiled a major update to its video-to-video model, SwitchX 2.0. The model's premise is to change what you want changed and keep what needs to stay.
This release adds native 4K output, clips up to 20 seconds at 24fps, and 10-bit color depth. Camera tracking has also improved, along with accuracy in handling fast motion and lip sync.

SwitchX is Beeble's own model for changing elements like lighting, background, and props while keeping the original subject and performance untouched. The company calls this release “our biggest upgrade yet to our video-to-video model.”

“SwitchX's core idea has always been simple: change what you want to change while keeping what needs to stay,” said Beeble founder and CEO Hoon Kim. “With SwitchX 2.0, we've extended that ability to longer, higher-quality sequences, giving increasingly ambitious productions the confidence to use AI.”

Among the new additions, output moved from 1080p to native 4K, maximum length increased to 20 seconds at 24fps, and color depth rose from 8-bit to 10-bit. Camera tracking improved so generated results follow the original footage's camera movement more closely. A new finishing workflow called Upres was also added: run quick, credit-efficient passes at 720p, then return to the original source to produce a final result at up to 4K.

Beeble also recently released a 3D scene generator built on World Labs technology. It builds Gaussian splat environments from text, images, video, or panoramas, lets users explore them in 3D, and extracts shots at up to 4K.

Recent updates also added Seedance 2.5 integration and SwitchHDR, which converts SDR footage into 16-bit HDR EXR. These features tie into Canvas, Beeble's node-based compositing environment, bringing generation, VFX, and finishing into a single workflow.
SwitchX 2.0 is available now on the Beeble platform. To mark the launch, generations made with the new model are 50% off through September 23, 2026.

Maggie Gyllenhaal says her experience sitting on juries from Cannes to Berlin has overlapped with her own shift from actor to director. “About ten days after finishing the final color mix on 'The Lost Daughter,' I went straight into being a Cannes juror.” This was during a conversation with IndieWire at the Hotel Excelsior on the Venice Lido.

“Having just finished my first film and then sitting down to watch the work of twenty-three interesting directors was an incredible experience. Being here now is definitely stimulating too.” Her term as president of the 2026 Venice competition jury ends this weekend.
Separate from her jury duties, she premiered her short film 'Flesh Impact' in Venice. It stars Ellen Burstyn, who received this year's Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement.

Made with Genesis, the project reunited her with Peter Sarsgaard and Dakota Johnson. 'The Bride!' cinematographer Lawrence Sher and 'The Lost Daughter' editor Affonso Gonçalves also came along. It was an exercise in imagining what Marilyn Monroe, marking 100 years since her birth, might say now.

The proposal came in while she was deep into editing 'The Bride!'. Last June marked Monroe's 100th birthday, and the pitch was to let this imagined Monroe act in ways she was never permitted to while alive. “They were surely picturing a young Marilyn Monroe. I thought, 'I don't really know much about Monroe.'”

After turning it over in her head for a while, the current idea emerged, and she wrote it very quickly. The deeper she dug, the more something like empathy for Monroe took shape, and she found points that overlapped with her own experience.

Asked whether it resembled 'The Bride!', she agreed. “Literally, I was making them at the same time. They're alike in that a dead famous figure comes back and says something different, something they might have been holding in their heart.”
The shoot was short. “I think I had about three and a half days with Ellen. It was very fast, so I needed people I already knew.”

The AI discussion came up when she revealed, during a local talk, that she had experimented with AI while making 'Flesh Impact.' She used only licensed images, though she added the caveat that the environmental cost still weighed on her.

“When I got the suggestion, I wasn't sure. Then I thought, 'No, let's learn.' I don't think there's anything you shouldn't even consider.” The result was clear. “It was a useless tool for this project. What I was looking for was exactly the opposite of what it offers. I was looking for the opposite of the icon, the very deep humanity attached to that iconic image. I was finding it in Dakota, but the moment you laid a machine-made layer on top of it, it vanished.”

She added that if it had actually been useful, that would have put her in a tougher spot. “I have such fundamental concerns and reservations about AI that I'd have landed in an ethical dilemma. I'm not an expert. I'm only just beginning to conceptually understand what AI even is. So I just dropped it.”
She also said the environmental issue can't just be tacked on as a single caveat and left at that. “That's a genuinely enormous problem. And so is the cultural dimension that comes with it.”

Kling AI opened the first-ever TIFF: The Market with a panel on opening morning, titled 'A New Creative Paradigm: Consistent, Cinematic AI Video Powered by Kling AI.' The room was packed. Canadian creators gathered, wanting to know where human craft still fits within a rapidly shifting production workflow.

blocks.cap: The Kling AI panel at TIFF: The Market

blocks.x: The panel was moderated by Tony Pu, who heads Kling AI's European and North American creator community and industry partnerships. It extended a conversation that began at a Cannes Film Market session, where Kling AI had announced it was joining 'Minibots,' Evolutionary Films' animated feature, as its global exclusive technology brand partner.

On stage were Diane Shorthouse, producer of 'Minibots' and co-founder of Evolutionary Films, and Issa Sissoko, an AI filmmaker who founded Amissa Studios. Sissoko has worked with Antoine Fuqua, Darren Aronofsky, and Doug Liman. Both teams use Kling AI's tools.
Shorthouse said a producer's core job, supporting the director's vision, hasn't changed. What's changed is the tools.

“The script is still the blueprint, so I think in terms of shots, not prompts.” Where the camera needs to go, what the performance should feel like, what the cut should land on. Then she weighs who can best pull it off and where to bring in an AI artist.

“We work out the visuals with the production designer first. If you generate twenty shots, nineteen of them will be wrong. But those nineteen matter, because recognizing what's wrong is a human judgment call.”

Sissoko helps directors and producers spot problems early, during previsualization, and decide what to shoot and where to spend money. “We also work alongside the VFX team. We build something in 3D and ask them to wrap a skin over it.”

The current challenge in hybrid production is relying less on raw model output, and blending AI with live-action footage seamlessly. “Handling AI so it preserves the actor's performance while adding something on top of it is very tricky.”

What both of them are waiting for in the coming months is more control. “I'd like it to listen to me a bit more.” The room laughed at that line from Shorthouse. “If I say put this character in this costume, in this setting, and just change where they're looking, I want it to change exactly that and leave everything else alone.”

Sissoko pointed to the pace of progress. “It gets dramatically better every 90 days. We've gone from 3-second generated clips to 15 seconds, and consistency has improved too.” He entered the industry making concept trailers, and said that when a pitch deck gets picked up because it came attached to a trailer, it creates work for a lot of people.

Shorthouse's advice to new directors was to learn the fundamentals hands-on first. “Know what shot you want, understand how camera, lighting, and performance work, and then experiment with AI. Put everything you know about filmmaking into the prompt.”
The most important skill, according to Sissoko, is writing. “Whatever you do, learn how to write a story first. It helps with prompting too.”

FutureCel Inc. and Curbside Entertainment have released the first footage from the animated comedy pilot 'The Salty Tales of Tony & Keith,' an original work made with generative AI animation. The release includes a one-minute teaser drawn from original art and AI-assisted animation, along with producer interviews.

blocks.cap: Key visual for 'The Salty Tales of Tony & Keith'

blocks.x: For Joel Kuwahara, this marks a new chapter. He left Bento Box Entertainment, the studio behind 'Bob's Burgers,' last September, a company he had co-founded in 2009. A 30-year veteran who came up through 'The Simpsons,' he sold Bento Box to Fox in 2019 and has now founded FutureCel Inc.

His partner is Mark Evestaff, an executive producer and showrunner who has worked on 'The Snoopy Show,' 'Jimmy Two Shoes,' 'Rocket Monkeys,' and 'Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs: The Series.' His Toronto-based studio, Curbside Entertainment, is co-producing with FutureCel.

The project was made by Canadian comedians Seán Cullen and Chris Locke, along with Evestaff. It began as a bit of improv comedy between Cullen and Locke, taking shape when the two recorded themselves ad-libbing in character as Tony and Keith during the pandemic. It's adult-oriented comedy about two characters who stay unfazed no matter how chaotic things get around them, and both comedians also voice their characters in the finished piece.

Kuwahara first saw the project through a message Evestaff sent on LinkedIn. The two found a way to compress a development process that usually takes years while still preserving what makes a pilot distinctive. “The comedy was unique because of the cast's improv. We never touched the dialogue at all. We just wanted to see these characters move.”
Evestaff said the principle was simple: “Follow what's funny.”

They went to Nura Studios and its platform Nura Showcraft, which recently opened public beta. The script, character designs, backgrounds, props, and storyboards were all drawn by human artists. Nura Studios director Elvis Deane took that material along with the recorded performances to build style sheets. “Working with the storyboards laid out alongside the recorded dialogue let us preserve both the hand-drawn style and the timing of the original performances.”

“Work that would normally take a week of back-and-forth with an outside artist, we knocked out sitting together in a few minutes,” Kuwahara noted. “That's when you realize how quickly you can move through the creative process.”

“Good projects die on the vine without ever getting past development,” Evestaff said. “Handled carefully, this technology lets you go further, fail faster, and start again. The creative work is still entirely human: the script, the storyboards, the character design. That's where the soul comes from. The tool just helps with execution.”
Kuwahara added, “This is a rich time to be a creator. AI was a big unlock. We get to make things with less, while holding more control.”
Mind The Gap Productions And Sales brought international rights to the period drama 'As Deep As The Grave' to TIFF: The Market. The film features the late Val Kilmer, brought back through AI.

blocks.cap: 'As Deep As The Grave' / Courtesy of First Line Films

blocks.x: Coerte Voorhees of First Line Films wrote and directed the film, about archaeologists chasing an ancient American civilization. John Voorhees produced, and the cast includes Abigail Lawrie, Tom Felton, Abigail Breslin, Wes Studi, Ewen Bremner, and Jacob Fortune-Lloyd.
Kilmer plays a priest trying to establish a new church. He had already been cast before the pandemic delayed production. In the time since, he became ill and died in 2025.
The production obtained permission from his family for the AI recreation, followed SAG-AFTRA guidelines, and paid compensation to his estate.

Mind The Gap founder Giulia Prenna said that “using AI is contentious, and it can never replace the authenticity of a performance a human actor truly lives through,” but added that “in this case, it was used ethically, with permission from Kilmer himself and his family. AI was an indispensable tool for honoring Val Kilmer's Cherokee heritage, his spirituality, and his wish to bring the role of Father Fintan to life.”

Mind The Gap's TIFF lineup this year also includes Robert Sayegh's thriller 'Beyond The Rush,' about an investigative journalist who goes undercover to expose a corrupt judge, starring Eric Roberts, Cathy Moriarty, and Mena Suvari.
Prenna's producing credits include 'The Fallout,' starring Jenna Ortega, which won the Best Narrative Feature and Audience Award at SXSW in 2021, and 'Office Uprising,' starring Brenton Thwaites.

Vicon, the motion capture division of Oxford Metrics, has acquired Captive Devices, based in Manchester, England. The company makes head-mounted camera systems that capture facial performance without markers. Vicon has supplied optical body tracking to film, game, and virtual production studios for more than 40 years, and now a facial piece has been added. Captive Devices' founding team joined Vicon immediately.
Its flagship product is CoreHMC. It captures facial data with a stereo head-mounted camera and feeds it directly into production pipelines, including Unreal Engine and MetaHuman Animator.
Studios such as Ninja Theory, Nant Studios, Animatrik, and Deep Silver Dambuster Studios already use it.
The deal brings markerless facial capture together with Vicon's marker-based body tracking under one roof. The company says it's the only one that builds and supports both systems in-house.

Marker-based tracking still sits at the center of Vicon's business. Customers can keep the equipment they already have and simply add markerless capability on top. Vicon introduced its own markerless body tracking system at GDC this past March.

David “Ed” Edwards, Vicon's head of entertainment and hardware products, said “this combination fills a real gap that film, game, and virtual production studios have been dealing with.” “Body and facial performance capture have always come from different vendors, through different pipelines. Now it's one system, one team, one point of support.”

Captive Devices co-founder Fred Isaac said that “joining Vicon gives us manufacturing scale, sales distribution, and a global support network. We'll be putting CoreHMC in front of far more studios than we could have reached on our own.” He added that the technology, the team, and the way they treat customers will all stay the same.

Oxford Metrics CEO Imogen O'Connor said “Vicon can now give customers a unified workflow spanning both body and face. Capturing, analyzing, and animating human performance now runs far more efficiently than before.”
Curious Refuge shares one of its favorite free AI tools for creating depth maps: Depth Anything, which can run locally on a Mac via a downloadable app or online through Fal.ai.

A depth map is a grayscale video in which shades represent how close or far objects are from the camera. In the tutorial, footage uploaded to Fal with the VDA Large model rendered a depth map in roughly 60 seconds.

The depth map is then used as a motion reference in an AI video tool, alongside a starting image for the look and the original footage, so the generated shot can change style and environment while following the original movement and spatial structure.

An AI-generated episode of Doctor Who was “pretty good,” according to BBC Director General Matt Brittin. The former Google EMEA boss said somebody had recently sent him a 50-minute episode of the long-running franchise that was completely AI-generated, and he refused to slam it. “I mean it’s not going to replace humans but we’ll come on to that,” he said.

Speaking at the RTS London Convention, Brittin echoed Amazon international boss Kelly Day in backing the power of AI: “Everyone’s [now] got the ability to create content almost at the standard of a Hollywood studio.” Days earlier he said he would allow a programme to be made and presented by AI “within guardrails.”
The talk came amid a £500M ($662M) BBC savings drive leading to hundreds of layoffs, with channel closures, possibly including BBC Three, expected soon.

Curious Refuge tested whether AI agents can handle sound design, running InVideo's new agent and ChatGPT Astra on footage whose original sound design had been removed, then comparing the results with the human-made versions across two projects.

InVideo placed some effects correctly but its execution was rough, with inconsistent leveling and choices that didn't fit the scene. Astra, which built the sound design inside Adobe Premiere Pro, produced the more useful result but still not professional quality. InVideo took about two hours and $4.56; Astra about 1 hour 45 minutes and $5.20.
The verdict: the tools are useful for a rough first pass a human can refine, but timing, emotion and creative intent still need a human.

LightBox Expo, founded in 2018 by Jim Demonakos and Bobby Chiu, returns to the Pasadena Convention Center October 23–25 with more than 200 sessions. Its strict no-generative-AI policy applies not only to panels but also to work sold in Artist Alley.

blocks.cap: Bobby Chiu, Jim Demonakos at the Annie Awards
