blocks.x: Demonakos said the expo has had an AI policy on its exhibit floor and in Artist Alley for four, possibly five, years: “We essentially consider AI work bootleg because you’ve stolen it from someone.” Last year it became attendee-facing. “We think generative AI is theft and it’s not real art.”

Asked about pushback from AI companies, he said there has been none, and artists have generally lauded the stance. Chiu said his own LightBox panel pushes back against AI by showing how to work with less time, fewer people and less money without using any AI.
Major studios including Disney, DreamWorks, Paramount, Illumination and Laika return year after year to recruit.

Mubi founder and CEO Efe Cakarel says the company is “going to stay as far away from AI as possible when it comes to films”, in a keynote at the Zurich Summit at the Zurich Film Festival on September 26.

“At Mubi, we’re going to use AI, and we are using AI in engineering, finance, operations, forecasting, customer service,” said Cakarel. He qualified the strategy: “Not because I believe AI cannot make something good. That argument is complacent and probably wrong. It is precisely because AI-generated content is about to become so good that human creation becomes more valuable.”

In the future, the value will be in “intention”, said the CEO, and in “taste, attention, cultural legitimacy, community, provenance, and above all, trust.” He warned that AI could lead to different versions of the same film being made for different viewers: “Hyper-personalised entertainment gives you satisfaction, but cinema gives you something to talk about.”

“So yes, we want machines doing a great deal of work in our lives; we just don’t want them making the movies. Because if I’m right about where entertainment is going, 20 years from now, the most radical thing a film company may be able to say is ‘This was made by people’.”

This month, Tonic DNA turned on a new website. “I call it a refresh more than a rebrand,” says partner Stefanie Bitton. Tonic DNA is a Montreal studio with roots reaching back about forty years: a traditional animation house, an IMAX pioneer, a 3D and hybrid shop, a director-led creative studio, and now a company with an original property in production and an AI pipeline built by its own artists.

blocks.cap: The reception at Tonic DNA in downtown Montreal.

blocks.x: “A renaissance suggests 2D disappeared. It never did,” Bitton says. This year the studio added The Anta Claus of the South Pole, a 24-minute 2D holiday special directed by Cordell Barker, co-produced with the National Film Board of Canada.

Tonic has spent two years building its own AI tools, and Bitton calls the approach AI with intention. “That doesn’t mean replacing the artist or skipping the craft. It means removing some of the friction around the process so the artists have more room to experiment.” The target is long-form 2D. “At first there was a lot of resistance,” she says, but the artists were involved in development. “Once the technology starts obscuring authorship or bypassing consent, you’ve crossed into a very different territory.”

blocks.cap: Concept art lines the lounge at Tonic DNA.
Official poster for ‘2026 Forum BIFF’ at the 31st Busan International Film Festival. / Photo courtesy of Busan International Film Festival

blocks.x: At the 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF), filmmakers from Korea and abroad will come together to discuss how artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the filmmaking environment, the crisis in Korean cinema, and the rights of film workers.
The festival's Jiseok Film Institute said it will hold ‘2026 Forum BIFF’ from October 8 to 11 at the Film and Video Industry Center and the Busan Viewers Media Center.

This year's theme is ‘Talking About the Possibilities of Contemporary Cinema.’ A total of 8 sessions will run across 4 areas: the film industry, AI and creation, systems and policy, and regions and environment.
Director Kim Jong-kwan, whose ‘Days and Nights to Each Other’ opens the festival, and Chinese director Jia Zhangke will give the keynote presentations.

The film industry sessions will look at why mid-budget Korean films are declining and discuss the potential for international co-productions. They will also cover the growth of Asian animation and the challenges ahead.

The AI sessions will examine the impact of generative AI on filmmaking and the role of creators. Related works will also be screened, including ‘Jia Zhangke's Dance,’ a short Jia Zhangke made with AI. Filmmakers from Korea and abroad, including director Min Kyu-dong, will take part.
The rights of film workers will also be on the table. Sessions will cover fair contracts, compensation and copyright, as well as ways to improve festival support programs.

The regional sessions will address how to sustain Busan's film industry. Key agenda items include cooperation between the film community and government bodies, and ways to cut carbon emissions during film production.
The forum is free and open to all, with no advance registration. It will be held in person only, with no online streaming.
The 31st Busan International Film Festival runs from October 6 to 15 around the Busan Cinema Center.

Tripo AI, the product brand of Beijing-founded VAST, came to SIGGRAPH 2026 with five technical papers, a keynote and a Real-Time Live! demo that won Best in Show. The company reports 20 million users and raised roughly $350 million this summer at a reported $1 billion valuation.

Chief scientist Yanpei Cao said the demo was built on SmartMesh, already in the product, optimized to generate game-ready assets with usable topology and texture in under two seconds per asset; in the shipping product it "takes less than five or 10 seconds." The company says its default is open source, across modeling, remesh, rigging, animation and texture.

Cao named four sectors: gaming, consumer 3D printing, film/animation/XR, and robotics. Major studios use the assets as reference, static props or environment blockouts, while small indie teams can now explore many more directions.

On film, Cao was direct: "the current quality of the output... is not to film-quality standards. But people are still using it," adding that previs "is a huge thing for us now." Tripo builds plugins for Maya, Houdini and Blender and is working toward an agentic system that automates tedious workflows, building AI "with the artists... not around them."

Artificial Intelligence isn't good at everything, but it is good at writing code. Small-scale software tools sit right in the sweet spot. Iain Anderson has no firm information on how the new tools he rounds up were made, but says it's a fair bet most had at least some degree of AI involvement.
Because coding has become easier, the post production scene is seeing a lot more apps that solve annoying smaller issues, because editors are able to design and implement those tools themselves.

blocks.cap: Beat turns your script into a node-based multifunctional document

blocks.x: Picks include Beat, a free visual scripting tool that can hook in AI tools via MCP, and PowerCue, a voice-activated teleprompter.

blocks.cap: Doza Assist is one of the current crop of AI-powered editing solutions

blocks.x: Automatic rough-cut tools such as Doza Assist, PowerCut and RoughCut also feature, alongside FCP Extender, which brings a generative extend feature to Final Cut Pro.
“There's still a big gap between ‘app made for me’ and ‘app that people will want to buy’,” Anderson writes, pointing to marketing and support as huge challenges.

Laemmle Theatres president Greg Laemmle and filmmaker and actor Raphael Sbarge host “Inside the Arthouse,” a video podcast that has grown to half a million YouTube subscribers and over 5 million views in two years.

The show has partnered with Chronicle, an AI-driven data company. Chronicle uses AI models to simulate audiences, analyze viewer behaviors and interest, push content more effectively to people on social, and tailor that data so the hosts can decide how to market and grow the podcast.

After two months, the hosts say engagement rose “literally almost overnight.” Chronicle builds an AI model trained on the show itself, then micro-targets clips to specific users rather than “buying a bunch of ads and just shotgunning it,” co-founder Scott Greenberg said.
The findings are shaping episode length, guest bookings and even potential live events in Laemmle's venues.
Generative AI is rapidly moving from experimentation into professional animation and commercial production. For studios, agencies and brands, the opportunity is significant.

blocks.cap: Ani, a small robot with glowing pink eyes, running across a desktop

blocks.x: But as AI becomes part of mainstream production, a more important question is emerging: what happens to the material being put into these systems? Creative teams routinely work with unreleased campaigns, proprietary characters, confidential footage and valuable client intellectual property.
Protections vary considerably between AI providers. Some commit not to train models on customer content; others retain broad rights over uploaded material.

Jon Draper, Creative Director for Generative AI at Synima and founder of AIAnimation.com, believes this will become one of the defining issues as AI animation matures. The next stage will be about professional infrastructure: clear ownership, controlled access, secure handling of client assets and transparency over how data is used.

EXCLUSIVE: Dubai’s MForMedia will look to add AI workflows into its productions following a deal with Arcana Labs. The two companies have struck a strategic partnership to incorporate Arcana’s software into MForMedia’s production workflows, Arabic-language co-productions and staff training. The overarching goal is to build AI-native film and television production capabilities across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region.

Arcana Studios, the production arm of Arcana Labs, and MForMedia will also co-produce original content for MENA audiences, with unnamed titles already in development. MForMedia staff are also provided with a five-day training workshop on AI-native production this month.

“With this model, we are embedding an AI-native pipeline inside a regional studio from day one,” said Arcana Labs CEO Jonathan Yunger. “Content can now be created in Dubai, in Arabic, faster and more cost-effectively than ever before, ensuring Arabic-language production stays in the region.”

MForMedia, led by co-founders and Managing Partners Ralph Matar and Khalil Homeissy, produces Arabic versions of Carpool Karaoke and The X Factor. The news comes soon after MForMedia hired MENA television industry veteran Ziad Kebbi as Managing Director, when the company announced it was pivoting toward AI production, original content and IP ownership.

blocks.cap: A still from Gods Don't Give Gifts

blocks.x: Popular YouTuber Gossip Goblin, aka Zack London, has released the trailer for his forthcoming film Gods Don’t Give Gifts, a feature film made entirely with artificial intelligence.

The sci-fi film will open in limited theatrical release in the U.S. and UK on December 4. The filmmakers say it is the first AI film to receive an MPA rating (R) and also to be campaigned in the Best Animated Feature category at the Academy Awards. The trailer goes to theaters on Friday, and billboard ads begin in November.
The film, previewed last month at the Venice Film Festival market, is produced by Edward Saatchi, whose AI company Fable counts Amazon among its backers.
“Gods Don’t Give Gifts is the first that has a shot at a nomination and then it’s all to play for,” Saatchi said. “We will be screening for voters and running a traditional campaign.”

SAG-AFTRA members will vote on a new four-year television animation agreement that includes annual wage increases, expanded AI protections, and improved streaming residuals for voice actors. The union’s Executive Committee has already unanimously approved the tentative 2026 Television Animation Agreement, negotiated with the AMPTP.
The contract guarantees a 3% wage increase in each of its four years, with the first increase retroactive to July 5, 2026.

As a point of priority, the agreement also expands AI protections, incorporating improvements negotiated in the union’s 2026 live-action agreements while retaining provisions specifically designed for animation performers. The previous animation contract, ratified in 2024, established the union’s first AI protections specifically for voice actors.

Performers would receive an average 5% increase in residuals when programs move to subscription streaming, and the subscriber factor for qualifying programs on large foreign streaming services rises from 39% to 41%. Employer health plan contributions rise 1%, with pension contributions up 1% from 2028 and 0.25% funding a new paid parental leave program.
Voting closes October 29 at 5 p.m. PT.

blocks.cap: Wētā FX’s Kora fire simulation toolset powered the combustion effects of Avatar: Fire and Ash. (Image courtesy of Wētā FX and 20th Century Studios)

blocks.x: AI may be the headline, but it’s only part of a broader shift. Real-time engines, virtual production, cloud workflows and increasingly intelligent systems are converging into a new kind of toolkit – one that compresses timelines, expands possibilities and shifts who holds creative control. VFX Voice asked artists, supervisors and technologists to identify the tools they believe will shape what comes next.

blocks.cap: ILM’s StageCraft LED volume on Thor: Love and Thunder

blocks.x: ILM’s Rob Bredow is most interested in art-directable machine learning: ML tools that act as assistants, filling in complex details in real-time as an artist draws, driven entirely by artistic choices rather than random generation.
Wētā FX CTO Kimball Thurston expects that in the short term generative AI will likely not be used for final pixels, as governance, quality and token cost issues compound to restrict usage.

blocks.cap: Beeble Canvas combines AI video models, node-based workflow automation and traditional compositing tools

blocks.x: Beeble AI CEO Hoon Kim sees a transition from AI as a purely generative tool toward AI as a controllable production system, while others point to Gaussian splatting, ML inside Houdini and Nuke, and real-time collaboration across post.

Three years ago, Jeffrey Katzenberg, co-founder and former CEO of DreamWorks Animation, predicted that the number of artists needed to make a world-class animated movie would decrease from 500 to less than 50 by 2026.

Joseph Bell’s Visual Effects & Animation World Atlas, built on over 1.1 million datapoints, finds that by mid-2026 AI has not yet replaced a significant number of roles at traditional VFX and animation studios, nor has it created many new ones. AI tools are being adopted by artists in their existing roles.

Globally, industry headcount increased 2.7% in the past 12 months. Los Angeles contracted by 1.5% while Vancouver rebounded by 11.3%. Average US VFX studio size fell from 34 to 29 people. Roto/paint roles increased 8.7%, suggesting AI is not yet ready to take over that work. AI-specific roles are just 0.1% of roles at traditional studios in 2026.
Can the same movie that required 500 artists back in 2023 be made by 50 artists today? “Not yet.”

Amsterdam-based creative production company Ambassadors has made its in-house visual AI workflow platform Mosa available now to all. First introduced in June, it was tested in a closed beta with 10 brands and agencies who built over 40 workflows and generated over 500 assets.

Mosa grew out of Ambassadors' own production work, where separate tools for images, video and upscaling meant prompts, data and brand requirements were carried by hand between them. It brings AI models, data and workflow steps into a single visual workflow that teams can reuse across projects, formats and markets.

“We built it because generating one good asset is no longer the hard part. The hard part is doing it consistently, across formats and markets, with the brand still intact,” says Diederik Veelo, CIO at Ambassadors.

Costs are visible at every step, and an AI agent helps users build workflows with no coding required. Mosa is now available to individual creators and freelancers as well as studios, agencies and in-house teams, with an enterprise plan for larger organizations.

As AI tools become better and easier to use, having clear context about the content you encounter online helps you make informed decisions about what to trust. Since launching Google SynthID in 2023, we've helped people identify AI-generated media using imperceptible watermarks across images, video, and audio. To date, we've watermarked over 180 billion images and videos, along with 240,000 years of audio content.

Last year, we introduced an early version of the SynthID Detector to help media professionals verify AI-generated content. Now, we’re expanding access to everyone – with the tool available globally in English starting today.
With the new SynthID Detector, anyone can easily check if an image, video, or audio file was made with AI from Google or our partners, including OpenAI, NVIDIA, Kakao, and soon, Apple.

This tool joins our built-in verification features in Search, the Gemini app, and Chrome, which now regularly handle over 1 million requests daily. It’s all part of our ongoing work to give you more context about the media you see online, so you can navigate the web with confidence.

A year after launching its AI production division Abundantia AiOn, India’s Abundantia Entertainment is morphing it into a fully standalone native AI studio that will seek to harness an influx of ideas from non-traditional sources.

“AiOn will develop its own stories, create its own content, produce fully generated as well as hybrid work, and manage the entire ecosystem, just as Abundantia does as a standalone studio,” founder and CEO Vikram Malhotra told Deadline. He said AiOn launches as a fully fledged studio in 2027.

Malhotra will lead AiOn for now. “For the moment, it will sit within Abundantia, but we are building it in a way that gives it its own identity and scope… It is truly a confluence of technology and art.”

He said that over the last six months he received “three times as many pitches from people who have never written, made films or belonged to the conventional filmmaking ecosystem” as in the past, citing directors such as Curry Barker and Kane Parsons as evidence of a “democratization” of ideas.
Earlier this year Abundantia also teamed with AI video company InVideo on a film studio developing a slate of five films.

Authors First, founded by private equity veteran Robert Hamwee, promises to let science-fiction and fantasy scribes adapt their titles as closely to their intended vision as possible. It uses AI generators like Seedance 2.5 and Nano Banana plus “other technology,” including Blender, to craft adaptations without the budget constraints of Hollywood studios.

The company launches after a more than $10 million seed round that includes Hamwee, Brand Foundry and The Family Office of David Blitzer. Hamwee leads as CEO, with a team including veterans of Hulu, Warner Bros. and Universal.

Its first project is “Genghis: Birth of an Empire,” adapting Conn Iggulden’s 2007 book “Wolf of the Plains.” Roughly 25 humans worked on the story, camera angles and dialogue, though the project was mostly generated by AI. Iggulden says it would never have been adapted otherwise, as offers fizzled over the budget a historical epic needs.

Just launched after a beta run, Sinima aims to be a new space for filmmakers and creators to host, protect, monitor, and earn on their films and videos, with a focus on what it calls “creative ownership.”

Launched by founders that include a former VP at Vimeo, Sinima targets two problems: creators can’t be sure whether their uploads are used to train AI models, while AI companies have limited legal avenues to train on real footage.

Features include hosting, private client review, ownership and provenance records, match monitoring, and creator-controlled AI permissions. Each upload gets a unique digital fingerprint and an ownership certificate with a public verification link, with details recorded in C2PA-format manifests.

When a title is licensed for AI training, creators keep 85% of what the buyer pays. The current rate card values eligible, rights-cleared footage at $4,000 to $7,500 per hour, so $3,400 to $6,375 per cleared hour goes to the creator.
Sinima is free to get started, with subscription plans starting at $15 a month.

blocks.cap: Image from Phil Tippett's 'Mad God' sequel now in production using LOFT. Image courtesy of LOFTAPPS.

blocks.x: Berkeley, California-based LOFTAPPS has announced that LOFT, its production software for generative AI, will make its European debut at VIEW Conference 2026, running October 12-16 in Turin, Italy. Attendees will also get an exclusive sneak peek at the sequel to Mad God, Phil Tippett's stop-motion feature, currently in production and powered by LOFT.

LOFT manages assets, creative intent, prompts, provenance, review, and production resources across complex pipelines and multiple AI models in a single system. Built as an AI-first product, it also supports hybrid workflows, and it is now shipping to select customers through a guided onboarding process.
"Its value is a connected production process that fundamentally changes how production work is generated, multiplied and managed," said LOFTAPPS co-founder and CEO Gary Mundell.

On October 15, Mundell and CTO Remko Noteboom, with Tippett joining remotely, present "The Hybrid Trap: Why AI-Native Production Matters," sharing behind-the-scenes content from AI-supported film projects that demonstrate the director's handmade visual style. Tippett spent some 30 years making Mad God, released in theaters in 2022.

Maxon has added built-in Model Context Protocol (MCP) support for Cinema 4D through the new Cinema 4D MCP server, letting artists use natural language instructions to securely direct Claude and ChatGPT or Codex AI assistants within Cinema 4D workflows.

“The idea is simple: Artists retain control while handing off any tasks they consider a chore,” says Maxon CEO David McGavran. Artists can use the assistants to organize hundreds of imported objects into a consistent hierarchy, create object and material variations, prepare multi-pass renders, and handle basic 3D camera tracking, UV mapping, rigging and animating.

Every action runs through Cinema 4D’s own API, in the artist’s own scene, on their own machine. Results remain native scene data, each batch of changes is broken down in the undo history, and commands are written to a local audit log. The server is protected by an access token, artists choose which tool groups the assistant may use, and Python execution can be controlled.
MCP is switched off by default and is available in Cinema 4D 2026.4 or later on Windows and macOS, with no additional installs.

blocks.cap: VFX supervisor Hong Jeong-ho presenting at the DFX Tech Show.

blocks.x: The DFX Tech Show is the flagship program of the Daejeon Special Effects Film Festival (DFX), where working professionals in the special-effects industry present industry and technology trends and behind-the-scenes production stories. At the September 18 session ‘What does not exist in reality, as if real-UNREAL’, the speakers were Jang Seong-ho, director at MOFAC Studio; Lee Jae-won, modeling supervisor at DreamWorks; and Hong Jeong-ho, VFX supervisor at Dexter Studios.

Director Jang said the term ‘chip valley’ is emerging in the industry and that “an era in which AI is actively used in video content production and AI solves many things on its own is just around the corner,” but that what ultimately matters is how well the creator's intent is realized. Supervisor Hong looked back on his work on <Gunche>, explaining that the recent trend is to use AI to make previs close in quality to the final output. At the September 19 ‘REAL’ session, art, martial arts and special makeup directors spoke about combining physical work with recent production.

On September 18, Daejeon City also held the awards ceremony for its AI video contest ‘Ai AI That Realizes Imagination vol.2’. Entries reached 504, up 139% from last year, and 19 winning works shared total prize money of 4800만원. Jury chair Son Seung-hyun, head of Westworld, said this year's judging focused on how complete and deep a story entrants built with AI as a tool.

The only surviving VHS tape of Messiah in Bethlehem, a 1994 concert performance, has been restored for theatrical projection. The only visual media ever shot in the church where Christ was born, the concert was a co-production of Israelis and Palestinians, with an audience of Christians, Muslims and Jews.

The work was done by DigitalFilm Tree (DFT) in Hollywood. Its CTO and senior colorist Thomas Galyon led the digital restoration, compositing and color, after the original cassette was digitized with time-based correction.

blocks.cap: Thomas Galyon at work on the restoration.

blocks.x: AI-based tools then tackled noise, blur, interlacing and instability: super-resolution from 480i toward 1080p or 4K, AI-assisted deinterlacing, noise reduction that separates real detail from analog noise, and transformer-based models that use neighboring frames for stabilization. Color was finished in DaVinci Resolve and compositing in Nuke, and the audio was repaired for hiss, hum and distortion.
“AI did not create the final product, Lost Treasure: Messiah in Bethlehem; it revealed it,” Galyon writes. The restoration was “an act of recovery, not invention.”

Ryan Serhant, the star realtor of Netflix’s “Owning Manhattan,” says his company produces about 2,200 social posts a month, with an in-house production studio of roughly 100 people. Now he has partnered with HeyGen to build a social media presence featuring an AI avatar modeled after his likeness, appearing on Instagram, TikTok and X as @HeySerhant to share lessons from decades in real estate.

“I’ve accumulated years of lessons that I don’t always have time to turn into content,” he tells Variety. “If you have a brand built around a face, if you have a brand built around a voice, how do you scale that?”

The account will produce at least one video a day for at least 12 months, with Serhant and his team working on each one. It won’t replace his personal content, such as “day in the life of a CEO” videos. The deal follows other figures licensing their likeness to AI companies, including Sunny Hostin with Fountain 0.
DittoDub launched its new Native 6 AI dubbing model, which now supports 109 languages, including 126 dialect options.

Launched as the new default dubbing model for videos uploaded on its platform, Native 6 is designed to be an easy, effective way for creators and video teams to carry a speaker’s voice, energy, and emotional delivery into a translated video.

“Viewers connect with a creator’s personality: how they tell a story or land a joke. When a video moves into another language, that personality should come with it. That is the standard we are building Native 6 around.” - Nate Stone, CEO and co-founder of DittoDub.
It works with the company’s existing video localization workflow: teams upload a recorded video, select their target languages, then review and edit the translated wording and vocals before sharing.

The platform also supports multiple speakers and prepares dubbed audio, subtitles, and translated video titles and descriptions. A YouTube Sync extension transfers these assets directly into YouTube Studio.
Native 6 is available now on DittoDub’s monthly subscription plans, starting at around $50 a month.
